blocks.h: ONLY DIAMOND CUTS DIAMOND
Roya Publication No. 108
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

Kian Sarrāf has an engine in him. He has had it since he was four, counting tiles in a Tehran basement while the bombs fell. Something catches his eye, the world goes quiet around it, and he does not come back until he has mastered it. A Rubik’s cube. Chess. A trading firm worth more than his father ever dreamed of. A 1967 Porsche rebuilt from three thousand bags of bolts.

His wife Roxana calls them his seasons. She writes each one on the calendar on the fridge, and when it ends she writes two words: Welcome back. For sixteen years he always comes back, to her, to their daughter Sahar, to their son Kaveh, to a long low house in a Los Angeles canyon that smells of hot clay on firing days.
Then, on the night he finishes the car, there is a curve on a mountain road.

Grief gives the engine nothing to hold. Until, at three in the morning, Kian learns that a laboratory can grow a diamond from what is left of a person. He decides that nobody will cut it but him. He leaves his children with his mother and goes to Antwerp, to the last hand-cutter on a street of armed guards and steel posts: Elias Karam, eighty years old, born in the diamond fields of Sierra Leone, who answers the last of thirty-one letters with four words.
Come. Bring nothing. E.
Elias teaches him the oldest rule of the trade. Every stone carries one tension. Find it before you cut, or it finds you.
Kian thinks he knows where his is.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

A warning first. This book contains graphic descriptions of cremation and of human remains, serious injury, the violence of a real war, and the grief of children. It does not offer comfort at the end. If you are carrying a fresh loss, it may be kinder to wait.
I have an engine in me. I don’t know when it started. I only know that it has always been running.

It works like this. Something catches my eye: a question, a skill, an old object, a problem nobody has solved. Then the world goes quiet. Everything that is not that one thing fades to grey. Sleep becomes optional. Food becomes fuel. Hours disappear and I don’t miss them. For a while, I am the happiest person alive.

Then I master it, or close enough. The engine has nothing left to chew. And the quiet I loved turns into a different kind of quiet, empty and loud at the same time. I have learned to dread that silence more than any failure. So the engine goes looking for the next thing. It always finds one.

People who live like this don’t choose it. I have come to believe it is closer to a temperament than a decision, the way some people are born tall. It has given me nearly everything I am proud of. It has also cost things I can’t count, because I was never looking at that ledger. Someone else was keeping it.
That is what this book is about. Not the obsession itself, which is easy to admire, but the people standing just outside it.

What I wanted to understand, and wanted the reader to feel, is how an obsessed mind actually thinks. Not as an illness or a superpower, but from the inside. How the people you love start to sound like interruptions. How “good enough” sounds like a lie. How you can love your family completely and still not hear what they are saying, because part of you is somewhere else, turning a stone over in the light.

And I wanted to turn the camera round. What does it feel like to be the wife who keeps the calendar of someone else’s seasons? The child who waits at the edge of a room for a parent to come back from a place they can’t follow? The people who love an obsessive are often the most patient people in the world, and their patience is rarely seen, because the one person who should notice it is busy.

The diamond seemed the right stone for this story. It is the hardest natural thing we know. Only another diamond can cut it. That felt true of obsession too. Only someone who has the engine can fully understand someone else who has it, and that understanding can be a comfort or a trap. Diamonds also carry a long human history of wanting: kings who killed for them, a slogan that taught the whole planet to desire them, a war paid for with them. Obsession is not a private flaw. It is one of the oldest things we do as a species.

The diamond trade, its methods and its history are real. The civil war in Sierra Leone and the mutilation of its civilians are real. Memorial diamonds made from a person’s ashes are real, and can be ordered today. Grief hallucinations, seeing or hearing someone who has died, are common and well recorded. The people in this book are invented, and so is the one turn the plot hangs on. I won’t say which, but you will know it when you reach it.

I don’t know whether the engine can be turned off. I am no longer sure I would want it to be. But I know now that it can be pointed. It can be aimed at a stone, or at a person. The second is much harder, because a person doesn’t hold still under the loupe, and is never finished, and was never meant to be.

I. ROUGH
The Little Engine
My name is Kian Sarrāf [kee-YAAN sar-RAAF]. The first thing I can remember is counting.

I was four years old and we were in the basement of our building in Tehran, because the city was being bombed. This was during the war with Iraq, which began the year before I was born and lasted until I was seven, so for most of my childhood the war was simply the weather. That spring, Iraqi planes came over the city at night. Most nights nothing happened. Some nights the radio stopped whatever it was playing and a man’s voice said, Attention, attention. The signal you are about to hear is the danger signal. It means an air raid. Leave your place of work or your home and go to a shelter. Then the siren went up over the rooftops, a long rising wail, and the radio called it vaz’iyat-e ghermez [vaz-ee-YAT-e gher-MEZ], the red situation. Every family in the building went down the stairs with blankets and a flask of tea and sat in the dark until the radio said the other words, vaz’iyat-e sefid [vaz-ee-YAT-e se-FEED], the white situation, which meant it was over.

The basement floor was laid in square tiles. I counted them. There were sixty-four between the boiler and the far wall, eight rows of eight. I counted them forward and backward. I counted the cracks in them. When the siren started I counted the seconds until the first sound of an impact, and when it came I started again from zero and counted until the next one.
My mother sat with her back against the wall and held me in her lap. She noticed that while I was counting I did not cry. She also noticed that the other children did.

“His little engine is running,” she told my father. She said it in Persian, motor-e kuchik [mo-TOR-e koo-CHEEK], and she said it the way you might talk about a dog that will not stop digging in the garden. With love, and a little bit of worry.

Here is the first thing I ever learned about my own mind, and I learned it before I could read. When it had one thing to hold, it stopped being afraid. It did not matter what the thing was. Tiles. Seconds. The number of times the man in the corner coughed. If I gave my mind one thing and nothing else, the whole loud world went quiet around it, and inside that quiet I was safe.
I have spent the rest of my life looking for that quiet. Everything in this book follows from it.
My father mended carpets.

Not new carpets. Old ones, hand-knotted, eighty and a hundred years old, from Kashan and Tabriz and the tribes in the south. People brought them to him torn, moth-eaten, burned by a dropped coal, chewed by a dog. He laid them face down on a long table in the back room of his shop and studied them through a magnifying glass, the way a doctor studies an X-ray. Then he rebuilt them, one knot at a time.

A good Persian carpet can have more than three hundred knots in a single square inch. My father would sit with one square inch for an entire day. He matched the wool to the old colours by eye, dyed it himself in pots on a gas ring, and tied each knot by hand with a hook no longer than his little finger. When he was finished you could not find the place where the damage had been. I used to try. I would run my hands over the carpet with my eyes closed, feeling for the scar, and never find it.
“A carpet forgives nothing and forgets nothing,” he told me. “So you do not make mistakes. You go slowly enough that there are none.”

On Fridays, when the shop was closed, he let me sit beside him and hand him the threads. He would name a colour, madder red, from the root of a plant, walnut brown, the blue that is almost black, and I would find it in the basket and lay it in his palm. If I chose wrong he did not scold me. He held the thread up to the window, held it beside the carpet, and waited for me to see the difference myself.
I always did, eventually. I would stare until I saw it.
My father never told me to stop staring. I think now that he was the only person in my life who never did. He had an engine too. His just ran slower than mine.
The worst of it came when I was six.

People who were in Tehran that year still call it the war of the cities. At the end of winter, Iraq stopped sending planes and started sending missiles: long-range rockets fired from far across the border, each one carrying a warhead about the weight of a motorbike. Over fifty-two days that spring, more than a hundred of them came down on Tehran. They fell by day and by night. They fell on neighbourhoods, markets and apartment blocks, because they were not aimed at anything smaller than the city.

A missile is different from a plane, and every child in Tehran learned the difference in a week. You could hear a plane coming. The siren had time to wail, the radio had time to say its sentence, and you had time to get down the stairs. A missile came faster than any of that. Sometimes the siren started after the explosion. Sometimes there was no siren at all, only a flat crack that shook the windows in their frames, and then, a few seconds later, every dog in the district barking at once.

So we stopped going upstairs. For most of that spring we lived in the basement. Forty people from eleven flats slept on the tiles, on carpets my father brought down from the shop, with our clothes on and our shoes beside our heads. The schools closed. The bakeries opened at dawn and were sold out by seven. Anyone who had a car, or a cousin in a village, or a sister near the Caspian Sea, left. By the middle of spring our street was half empty, and people said a quarter of the whole city had gone. Nobody knew the real number. There was nobody left to count.
Except me. I counted.

I kept a school exercise book under my pillow in the basement. Every time I heard an impact I made a mark in it, with the time, if I could see the boiler-room clock, and a word for how it sounded: far, near, very near, the windows. When the radio read out where a missile had landed, I wrote the name of the district beside the mark. When the radio gave a number of dead, I wrote the number in the margin and added it to the total at the top of the page.
I did not think of the numbers as people. I want to be honest about that, because it is the first time it happened and it was not the last.
They were numbers, and numbers were safe, and the total at the top of the page went up every day like a score. Keeping it tidy made me feel that someone, somewhere, was in charge.

One night, very near, a missile came down three streets away. The basement shook and white dust sifted down from the ceiling onto the blankets. A woman screamed. The baby from the third floor began to cry and did not stop for an hour. My mother pulled me against her so hard I could feel her heart going against my back, fast and hard, like something trying to get out.
“Hold my hand,” she whispered. “Kian. Hold my hand.”
I didn’t. I needed my hand to make the mark.

She took the exercise book from me in the morning, while I was still asleep. I woke to see her sitting on the bottom step in the grey light with it open on her knees, turning the pages slowly. She had reached the total at the top of the last page. Her lips were moving. She was reading it the way you read a name on a gravestone.

She did not scold me. She closed the book, and put it back under my pillow, and went upstairs to see if there was bread. But she did not call me her little engine again for a long time, and when she did, years later, she no longer said it as a joke.

That spring my father did not close his shop. He said that the carpets did not know there was a war. Every morning he walked the eleven streets to the bazaar and sat at his long table under the bare bulb, re-knotting a Kashan with a burn hole in it the size of a fist, while the windows rattled in their frames. He took me with him twice, when my mother was too tired to argue. I sat under the table and handed him threads.

Once, a missile came down close enough that the bulb swung on its wire and the shadows of the table legs swung with it, back and forth across the floor. My father’s hook stopped for a moment above the knot. Then he finished the knot.
“How far?” I asked him. I wanted it for the book.
He looked at me under the table for a long time.
“Ask me how many,” he said. “Not how far. How many.”
I didn’t understand him. I said, “How many?”
“Too many,” he said, and tied the next knot.

The missiles stopped in the spring. The war stopped that summer. We left Tehran a few weeks later, the summer I was seven. My father sold the shop and the tools and most of the carpets. He kept one, a small prayer rug with a hole in its corner that he had never got round to fixing. He said he would fix it in America.
He never did. It is on the floor of my front hall now, in Los Angeles, with the hole still in it.

I have thought about that hole more than I have thought about almost anything. A man who could rebuild a hundred-year-old carpet so that nobody could find the scar, and he left one hole open, in his own rug, for thirty years.
I did not understand it until very recently. I will come to it.
Westwood

We lived in two rooms above a dry cleaner on Westwood Boulevard. The street was full of Iranian shops and Iranian restaurants and Iranian men arguing outside the bakery in the mornings, so many that people called the neighbourhood Tehrangeles. My father opened a small repair shop two blocks down. My mother worked the counter at a pharmacy and learned English faster than any of us.

In the first month I sorted my father’s threads. He kept them in three old biscuit tins, four hundred skeins of wool all tangled together, and one Saturday while he was out I sorted every one of them by colour, from the palest cream to the blue that is almost black, in a long line across the floor of the shop. It took me six hours. I was very proud.

He came back and looked at it for a while. He said it was beautiful. He left it that way for a week. Then one evening I saw him on his knees, quietly putting them back in his own order, which was not by colour at all. It was by how often he reached for them. The ones he used most were nearest his hand.
He never said a word about it. I understood it about thirty years later.
I did not speak English when I arrived. So I learned it the only way I knew how. I took a paperback dictionary from the library and started at A.

I did not learn words. I learned the dictionary. I read it the way other children read comics, under the blanket with a torch. By Christmas I was at M. My teacher called my parents in to ask how a boy who had arrived in September was using the word meretricious, which means showy and cheap, in a spelling test. My mother did not know what it meant either. She looked at me across the little table with the same face she had worn in the basement, the dog-in-the-garden face, and said nothing all the way home.
When I was nine, a neighbour gave me a Rubik’s cube for my birthday.

If you have never held one: it is a plastic cube, a little bigger than a fist, with six faces in six colours, each face divided into nine squares. You twist the rows and the colours scramble. The puzzle is to twist them back.

There are forty-three quintillion ways to scramble it. Forty-three followed by eighteen zeroes. I know because I looked it up that first night, and the number frightened me and delighted me in exactly equal parts.
It took me twenty-nine days to solve it without help.

I did not eat breakfast. I did not hear my mother calling me. I did my homework in the five minutes before class and twisted the cube under the desk with my other hand. I dreamed in colours. I stopped seeing my friends. By the third week I could see the cube with my eyes closed, all six faces at once, the way you can see a room in the dark if you have lived in it long enough.
On the twenty-ninth night, at about eleven o’clock, the last corner turned into place and every face was one colour.
I remember the feeling exactly. It went through me like warm water. It was the best feeling I had ever had in my life, better than Christmas, better than anything, and it lasted about four minutes.
Then it was gone. And something else came in behind it.

I did not have a word for it then. I have one now. I call it dead air. It is the phrase radio people use for the silence when a station has nothing to broadcast. That is what it feels like. The engine is still running, but there is nothing in front of it. The quiet I loved, the safe quiet of one thing, turns into a different quiet. It is empty and it is loud at the same time.

I put the cube on my desk. The next day I could not look at it. I could not bear to have it in the room, this thing that had been the whole world for twenty-nine days and was now just a plastic toy. I gave it to a boy in my class. He was very pleased.
My mother found me lying on my bed with my shoes on, staring at the ceiling.
“What’s wrong?” she said.
“Nothing.”
She sat on the edge of the bed. She did not touch me. She knew better.
“It will find something else,” she said. “It always does.”
She was right. It always did.
Sixty-Four Squares
At fourteen it found chess.

A teacher set up a board at lunch to teach a few of us the moves. I watched for ten minutes. Then I went to the library and took out every chess book they had, eleven of them, and carried them home in two plastic bags.
The board is eight squares by eight. Sixty-four. The same as the basement floor in Tehran. I did not notice that until years later, and when I did, I had to sit down.

I want to tell you what the next two years were like, because it is the clearest example I have of how my mind works. Years later I gave the stages names, and I will use them now so you can see the shape.
The first stage is the hook. Something catches. It is never something I go looking for. It is a door left open in a corridor, and I glance through it, and I am already inside.

The second stage is the narrowing. The world begins to shrink. At first it is pleasant, like the lights going down in a cinema. Everything that is not the one thing fades to grey. Food becomes something I do so that I can keep going. Sleep becomes something I do when I can no longer see the board. And people, and this is the part that is hard to say, people become interruptions. I loved my parents. I loved my friends. But when my mother called me for dinner, what I felt was not love. It was the feeling you have when someone talks to you during the best part of a film.

The third stage is the burn. This is the part outsiders see and cannot understand. No sleep, no food, sixteen hours a day, and I was not suffering. I was the happiest I have ever been. That is the thing nobody tells you about obsession. From the inside it does not feel like a sickness. It feels like being completely alive.
The fourth stage is the summit. Mastery, or something close to it.
The fifth is dead air.

By fifteen I was playing in adult tournaments on weekends. By sixteen my rating was a few points short of the title of master. I played my father in the evenings, on a board I had set on top of one of his repair jobs, a Bakhtiari rug with a garden pattern. He was a terrible player and he never minded. He would watch my face while I thought. I didn’t know he was doing it. He told me so much later.
“You looked,” he said, “like a man listening for something very far away.”

The summer I was sixteen I missed his fiftieth birthday. There was a weekend tournament in San Diego. I had told my mother I would be back for dinner and I was not. I was in the final round, in a position I had studied for a month, and I did not think about my father or his birthday once. I did not think about anything. That was the point.

I won. I came home at midnight with a small trophy and found the cake on the table with fifty candles in it, none of them lit. My father was asleep in his chair. My mother was washing the dishes, slowly, the way you wash dishes when you want somebody to notice you washing them.
I stood in the doorway holding the trophy. And for the first time in my life I saw the shape of what I had done from the outside. Not the game. The empty chair at the table, kept for me all evening.
I felt ashamed. It was a real shame and it went deep.

And here is the second thing I learned about my mind, and it is uglier than the first. Even standing there ashamed, some part of me was still replaying the final position. Some part of me was checking whether my knight had really been safe on the twenty-third move.
I quit chess two weeks later. Not because of the shame. I quit because I had reached the top of what I could do on my own, and the dead air came in, and the board looked like a piece of painted wood.
I gave the books back to the library. All eleven. They were very overdue.
The Firm

I studied mathematics at UCLA, which surprised nobody. I did very well, which surprised nobody either. I had a handful of friends, and I was not easy to be friends with. I would vanish for a month into a problem set and come out blinking, like a man from a cave, and expect everyone to be exactly where I had left them.
Mostly they were. People are kinder than they need to be.

At twenty-six I started a trading firm with two men I had met in a graduate seminar. I will not tell you their names. They are not part of this story and they would not want to be. What we did, in plain words, was teach computers to notice tiny patterns in the prices of things and to buy and sell faster than any human could. It was a puzzle with real money on the other side of it. It was the Rubik’s cube with forty-three quintillion dollars attached.
The hook caught in the first week. The narrowing took about a month. The burn lasted, with short breaks, for eight years.

I worked ninety hours a week. I slept on a couch in the office three or four nights out of seven. My mother learned to call the office number instead of my flat, and to start every call with the words I know you’re busy, so I would not have to say it. I ate the same lunch every day for two years, a turkey sandwich from the same shop, because choosing lunch was a decision, and I did not want to spend a decision on lunch.

We made money. Then we made more money than I had known existed. In the third year I bought my parents a house in the hills above Encino, with a garden and a lemon tree. My mother cried in the driveway. My father walked through every room, slowly, and then asked if there was space in the garage for a long table.

He kept working. He never stopped. At sixty-five he was still re-knotting other people’s carpets in that garage, with the door open for the light, while the lemons dropped in the yard. I offered to pay him to retire. He laughed at me.
“Retire and do what?” he said. “Sit?”
I understood him perfectly. It was the most I ever felt like his son.
I had been running the firm for about a year when I met Roxana.
Good Enough

It was a ceramics show in an old warehouse in Venice, near the beach. A friend had dragged me there. I hated crowds and I didn’t care about pottery, and I stood near the door with a plastic cup of wine planning how soon I could leave.
Then I saw the bowl.

It sat by itself on a wooden plinth near the back. It was small, about the size of two cupped hands, and the glaze was a deep grey-blue that went almost black at the rim, like the sea just after sunset. It was not perfectly round. One side rose a little higher than the other, as if the bowl had leaned to listen to something.

I looked at it for a long time. I was looking for the flaw. That is what I do with beautiful things. I look for the place where they went wrong, because if I can find it, I can understand how they were made.
“There’s a crack,” said a woman beside me. “Inside the foot. You can’t see it.”

She was about my age. She had clay dried on her forearms, and her hair was tied up with a pencil stuck through it, and she was looking at me with open amusement, the way you look at a man who has been staring at a bowl for six minutes.
“Then how do you know it’s there?” I said.
“Because I made it.”
She picked the bowl up and turned it over to show me. I still couldn’t see anything.
“I’d fix it,” I said, before I could stop myself.
“I know you would,” she said. “You’ve got that face.” She put the bowl back on its plinth. “But it holds water. It holds soup. It’s good enough. That’s the best thing a bowl can be.”
Good enough. I had never in my life heard those two words put together as praise.

Her name was Roxana [rok-SAA-na]. Her parents had come from Shiraz before the revolution, and she had been born in Los Angeles and spoke Persian with a California accent that my mother would later find unbearably charming. She made bowls and cups and plates in a rented studio in Mar Vista. She made them until they were good enough, and then she stopped, and then she made the next one.
She gave me the bowl. She would not let me pay for it. “You’ll just stare at it,” she said. “That’s better than money.”
I have it still. I have never found the crack.
I was a terrible boyfriend. She told me so, cheerfully and often.

I forgot dinners. I disappeared for days into the firm and came out surprised that the weekend had passed. Once, in the first year, I cancelled a trip to Big Sur at four in the morning because a model was misbehaving, and she drove up alone, and sent me a photograph of the sea with no message, and that was the message.
Any other woman would have left. Roxana did something stranger. She studied me.
She studied me the way my father studied a carpet, patiently, without blame, looking for the pattern. And after about a year she found it.
I came home one night at three in the morning. She was sitting up in bed with a sketchbook.
“What season is this?” she said.
“What?”

“You have seasons,” she said. “Like weather. I’ve been watching. Something grabs you and you go away into it, and you’re gone for a month, or a year, and you come back thin and happy, and then you’re sad for a while, and then something else grabs you. It’s a season.” She tapped the sketchbook with her pencil. “So which one are we in?”
Nobody had ever seen it that clearly. Not my mother. Not even my father, who saw it but never said it out loud. I sat down on the bed in my coat and could not speak.

The next morning there was a calendar on the fridge. A big paper one, a month to a page. Across the top of October she had written in green marker: THE MODEL SEASON. Expected end: unknown. Bring snacks.

She kept it up for sixteen years. Every season got a name and a colour. When one ended she drew a small line across the bottom of the month, and on the next day, without fail, she wrote two words: Welcome back.

She never once asked me to be different. That is the thing I want you to understand about her, before anything else in this book. She did not ask me to stop. She asked me to come back between seasons.
And I always did. I always came back.
The one time I tried to buy her a diamond, I made a season of it.

I spent four months learning about diamonds before I proposed. I read everything. The four Cs: cut, colour, clarity, carat. How a round stone is cut with fifty-seven or fifty-eight flat faces, called facets, angled so that light goes in through the top and bounces around inside and comes back out at your eye. I learned that the mathematics of that bounce had been worked out in 1919 by a young engineer named Tolkowsky [tol-KOV-skee]. I learned that a diamond is only carbon, the same element as pencil lead and coal, squeezed for a billion years in the dark.

At a jeweller’s in Beverly Hills an old man let me look at a stone through his loupe [LOOP], a little magnifying glass you hold right up to the eye. Inside the diamond, very small, I saw a flaw. It looked like a white feather, frozen in the middle of the stone, as if something had been falling through it when the stone set hard around it.
I looked at that feather for twenty minutes. The jeweller let me. I think he had seen the face before.

Then I bought the stone and asked Roxana to marry me, and she said yes, and then she laughed and said she could not wear a diamond ring in the studio because it would get full of clay and she would lose it in a pot. So she wore it on a thin chain around her neck, for the rest of her life, and she wore a plain gold band on her finger instead.
The diamond season ended the day she said yes. I didn’t think about diamonds again for nearly sixteen years.
But I want you to notice something. The hook didn’t fail to catch. I remember that feather. I can still see it if I close my eyes. The hook had caught. It was only waiting.
The House

We were married in her parents’ garden in the summer. My father wore a suit for the first time since Tehran and danced with every woman in the family. My mother cried, as she did in driveways, at weddings and at good news of any kind.

Halfway through the evening I noticed that the band’s violinist was playing very slightly flat, a hair under every note, and once I noticed, I could not hear anything else. Roxana felt it happen. She always could. She found my hand under the table and pressed it twice, which in the language we had by then meant not tonight. I let it go. It was hard, and I did it for her, and I think it was the best wedding present I gave her.

Sahar [sa-HAR] was born the next year. Her name means dawn, because she came at ten past five in the morning, after a long night, and the window of the hospital room turned grey and then pink while Roxana held her. Through most of that night I timed her contractions on a stopwatch, to the tenth of a second, and read the numbers out. Around three in the morning she took the stopwatch out of my hand and threw it across the room, and the nurse laughed, and I held Roxana’s hand instead. It was the right thing. I had to be shown it.
I am going to tell you how I loved my daughter, because later in this book you will need to remember it.

I loved her so much it frightened me. In her first month I did what I always do with something I love: I tried to understand it completely. I kept a spreadsheet. I logged every feed, every nap, every nappy, and the colour of what was in it. I drew graphs of her sleep. I read eleven books about infant development, the same number as the chess books, which I noticed and did not like.
On the twenty-fourth day Roxana came into my study at three in the morning with Sahar on her shoulder. She looked at the graphs on my screen. Then she closed the laptop, gently, with one hand.
“She isn’t a model,” she said. “She’s a baby. Come and hold her.”

I did. Sahar was warm and heavy and smelled of milk, and she fell asleep against my neck with her small fist closed on my collar. I stood in the dark kitchen holding her for an hour. I did not count anything. It was one of the few hours of my life when the engine was simply off.
On the fridge, Roxana wrote: THE SPREADSHEET SEASON. Ended by force. Under it she drew a baby with a crown.

Sahar grew up funny. That was the main thing about her. She was funny before she could talk. She had her mother’s habit of watching me with amusement, and by the age of six she had her mother’s habit of saying what she saw.
“Baba [baa-BAA] is in a season,” she would tell visitors, gravely. “We don’t talk to him until it’s over.”

She read the fridge calendar the way other children read comics. She knew the names of all my seasons. When she was eight she started adding her own captions in pencil under her mother’s. Under THE MIRROR SEASON, which was the year I spent grinding a telescope mirror by hand in the garage, she wrote: He talks to it. It does not talk back.
She was right. I did talk to it.

That was the year she played a tree in her school play. She had one line. I was there, in the third row, and I want that written down, because I was not always there. But I spent most of the play working out in my head the curve I would need to grind into the mirror that night, and when she said her line I was a fraction of a second late looking up. She saw. Children always see. Afterwards, in the car, she asked me what her line had been. I told her. I had heard it. She nodded and looked out of the window and did not ask me anything else.

My father died in the winter of the mirror season, two years after I sold the firm. He was seventy. His heart stopped at his long table in the garage in Encino, with a Tabriz half-mended in front of him and the hook still in his hand.

He did not die at once. There were three hours in the hospital. My mother called me four times. I was in our garage with the phone face down on the workbench, because its buzz shook the mirror, and I had reached the part of the grinding where you cannot stop or the glass is spoiled.

I got there in time. I want that written down too. I arrived forty minutes after everybody else, and he was still awake. He looked at my hands, which were grey to the wrist with glass dust, and he smiled, as if that told him everything about where I had been. He did not seem angry. He seemed to recognise it.
“Did you finish?” he asked.
I said I had.
“Good,” he said. “Then sit.”
I sat with him until the morning. I did not count anything.
I never used the mirror. It is still in its box in the garage.
I sold my share of the firm when I was thirty-four.

I had reached the summit. There was nothing left in it I did not understand, and when I understood it completely, the dead air came in, and the most profitable business I would ever build looked to me like a piece of painted wood.
My partners thought I was mad. Roxana did not. She had seen it coming for months. She had already written on the calendar, in advance, in pencil, THE FIRM — ending soon?

What came after was the worst dead air of my life. For four months I did nothing. I sat in the garden. I lay on the floor of my study. I could not read, because reading is a task, and the engine refused any task that was not the right one. I lost weight. I stopped answering the phone. My mother came over and cooked and watched me with her basement face.

Roxana did not try to fix me. She knew it could not be fixed, only waited out. She went to the studio and came home and sat beside me in the garden in the evenings and talked about her day, about a glaze that had run, a kiln that had cracked a whole shelf, a customer who wanted a bowl the exact colour of her dog. She did not need me to answer. She just kept the sound of a life going near me, like a radio left on in a sick room.
That winter Kaveh [kaa-VEH] was born. We named him after the blacksmith in the old Persian Book of Kings, the poor man who stood up to a tyrant and raised his leather apron on a spear as a flag.

The night we brought him home, the dead air lifted. It did not go all at once. But I held him in the same dark kitchen where I had held his sister, and I felt the engine start again, slowly, the way a car starts on a cold morning.
Here is our house, in the years before. I want you to see it.

It is a long, low house in the hills of Topanga, at the end of a dirt road, with oak trees and a view down the canyon toward the sea. There is a studio for Roxana at the bottom of the garden, with a kiln in a shed beside it, and on firing days the whole place smells of hot stone. There is a double garage, and the left half of it is mine.

There is a fridge in the kitchen, and on the fridge there is a calendar, and on the calendar are my seasons, in Roxana’s handwriting, sixteen years of them, the old ones kept in a box under the stairs.

THE CHOPIN SEASON, which was the year I tried to learn one piano étude [ay-TOOD], a study piece, a fast, cruel one Chopin wrote at nineteen, and practised it six hours a day until my wrists ached and I could play it at the speed he asked for, once, on a Tuesday afternoon with nobody listening. Then never again.
THE BREAD SEASON, which was short and which everyone enjoyed.
THE MIRROR SEASON. THE LATIN SEASON. THE SEASON OF THE BEES, which ended badly, with the bees.
And the long one, the one that was running in the summer this story turns. THE CAR.

Nowruz [now-ROOZ] is the Persian New Year. It falls on the first day of spring. Every Iranian family lays a table for it, called the haft-sin [haft-SEEN], with seven things on it whose names begin with the Persian letter S: wheat sprouts for new life, garlic for health, apples for beauty, and so on. There is a mirror, and a bowl with a goldfish in it, and painted eggs.

Our last Nowruz together, my mother came up the canyon with a tray of sweets and the gold tea spoon she had carried out of Tehran in her handbag. It was the only gold thing she brought. She set it beside the mirror on the haft-sin every year, polished, because it had been her own mother’s.

Sahar was nearly fifteen that spring. She painted the eggs and wrote rude words on them in tiny letters, and then turned the rude sides to face the wall so her grandmother would not see. Her grandmother saw. Her grandmother laughed so hard she had to sit down.
Kaveh was nine. He did not paint eggs. He was busy.

Kaveh had sorted all his Lego by colour into ice-cube trays. He had borrowed every ice-cube tray in the house, and two from the neighbours, and lined them up across the living-room floor: red, orange, yellow, green, the three different blues, and the grey that Lego calls dark bluish grey and that he insisted on calling by its full name. He was not building anything. He was sorting. He had been sorting for three days.
At some point Sahar, passing, picked a red brick out of the red tray and dropped it into the yellow one as a joke.

Kaveh screamed. Not a tantrum scream. A scream of real pain, as if she had stepped on his hand. He found the brick, put it back, and then checked every tray on the floor, one by one, with his lips moving, until he was sure nothing else was wrong.

Sahar stood there frozen, holding her paintbrush. She looked across the room at me. I will never forget that look. She was not asking me what was wrong with her brother. She was asking me whether I knew.

I knew. I stood in the kitchen doorway and I watched my son count his trays with his lips moving. I felt pride, a fierce warm pride, because I saw myself in him. And under the pride I felt something cold. It was the feeling of watching someone you love walk toward a door you know very well.
Roxana came up beside me, wiping clay off her hands.
“He’s yours,” she said softly. She did not sound worried. She sounded like a woman reading the weather. “We’ll keep an eye on it.”

That night I read to him at bedtime. He liked me to read the chess books aloud in voices. I had a voice for every piece. The bishop was a grumpy old man who could only walk diagonally and complained about it constantly. The knight was a show-off who jumped over everyone. The pawns were nervous.
“Do the bishop,” Kaveh said.
“I can only go slantways,” I said, in the bishop’s voice. “My whole life. Slantways. Forty years of slantways. Do you know what that does to a man’s knees?”
Kaveh laughed until he got the hiccups. I sat by his bed until he fell asleep, with his hand still curled around a single red brick he had taken to bed with him, to keep it safe.
In the summer Sahar taught Kaveh to swim at Zuma beach.

She had learned there herself, at five, with Roxana holding her flat on the surface of the water and walking her slowly out past the breakers. Now she did the same for her brother. She was strict and patient and she shouted at him in the voice of a gym teacher, and he did everything she said, because she was his sister and fifteen, and because, I think, he worshipped her.
Roxana and I sat on a towel and watched. Or Roxana watched. I was on my phone, reading a forum thread about valve springs for an air-cooled engine built in 1967.
“Kian,” she said. “Look at them.”

I looked. They were a long way out. Sahar was holding Kaveh flat on the water, the way her mother had held her. The sun was going down behind them and the sea had turned that grey-blue that goes almost black, the colour of the bowl.
“When I go,” Roxana said, “I want to go out there. Past the kelp. Where she learned to swim.”
“Mm,” I said.

I was reading about valve springs. I heard her. I heard the words. I did not take them in. That is the honest truth and I am putting it here because I promised myself, when I began to write this, that I would put the honest truth everywhere I could find it.
“Mm,” I said. And went on reading.
She didn’t repeat it. She didn’t need to. She had said it to the sea, not to me, and the sea was listening.
First Drive

The car was a 1967 Porsche 911, red, the colour the factory called Polo Red. I bought it from a man in Bakersfield for almost nothing. It had sat in a field for twenty years. There were mice living in the seats and a tree growing through the floor of the boot.

I took it apart in the left half of our garage. Every bolt. I photographed each one before I removed it, labelled it, and stored it in a numbered bag. There were three thousand, one hundred and sixty bags. They hung from wires across the ceiling of the garage like a strange harvest, and when the wind blew down the canyon they turned slowly and clicked against each other.
It took me three years.

I rebuilt the engine by hand. I rebuilt the gearbox. I learned to weld. I learned to shape metal with a hammer over a leather bag of sand. I tracked down original parts in Germany, in Japan, in a widow’s barn in Ohio. I learned more about that car than the men who designed it had ever needed to know.
Roxana wrote THE CAR across the top of the calendar in red marker, the first season she had ever written in red, and under it she drew a small car with a question mark for a driver.
“Who’s going to drive it first?” she said. “When it’s done.”
“Me,” I said.
“We’ll see,” she said.
Sahar asked me the same question that summer, in a different way. She was fifteen and about to get her learner’s permit, and she came into the garage one evening and stood watching me set the valves.
“Can I learn on it?” she said. “When it’s finished?”
“Nobody drives it but me,” I said, without looking up. “Not even your mother.”

I said it lightly. I meant it as a joke about how careful I was. She didn’t laugh. She stood there a moment longer, then went back into the house, and I heard her tell Kaveh, in the kitchen, in a voice I was not supposed to hear, don’t bother asking.
I noticed that. I put it in the part of my mind where I keep things to deal with after the season ends. That part of my mind is very full. Things go in and they do not come out.
I finished it on a night in early September.

I had been awake for about forty hours. That was not unusual at the end of a season. The last stretch is always the worst and the best: the summit in sight, everything narrowed to a single point, the body forgotten. I had been fitting the last trim pieces since the morning before. My eyes were sore. My hands had stopped feeling like mine. None of it mattered.
At two in the morning I took the last bolt out of the last bag, and fitted it, and turned the key.

The engine caught on the first try. It made a sound I cannot describe properly. An air-cooled flat-six has a voice like nothing else, a dry rising snarl, and it filled the garage and rang off the walls and set every one of the three thousand empty bags spinning on its wire.
I sat in the driver’s seat with my hands on the wheel and I laughed. I could not stop.
Then the side door opened, and Roxana came into the garage in my old university sweatshirt, barefoot, her hair down, laughing too.
“You did it,” she said. “You actually did it.”

She walked all the way around the car slowly, the way my father had walked through the new house. She ran her hand along the curve of the roof. Upstairs, through the little garage window, I could see the light in Sahar’s bedroom. She was awake. She was always awake at two in the morning that summer, on her phone, the way fifteen-year-olds are.
“Take me for a drive,” Roxana said.
“It’s two in the morning.”
“That’s the best time,” she said. “Nobody on the roads. Up the Crest. Come on. The kids are asleep. Well, one of them.”
I should tell you how it went next, and I am going to tell it the way I remember it.

She wanted to drive it first. She had always said she would, and now she said it again, standing by the door in her bare feet, holding her hand out. I remember the keys in her hand. I remember her climbing into the driver’s seat and pulling it forward, because she was shorter than me, and laughing at how low the seat was, and saying that it smelled like my garage, which was true.

We drove down the canyon and across the sleeping city and then up into the San Gabriel mountains on the Angeles Crest Highway, the long, empty, twisting road that climbs above Los Angeles into the pines. The Crest road, everyone calls it. At that hour there was nothing on it. The whole city lay below us, an enormous field of orange lights going all the way to the sea, and above us the stars came out one by one as the city’s glow fell away.
She put her arm out of the window and let the cold air push against her hand. She was singing something under her breath. I don’t remember what. I have tried and I cannot.

I remember being happy. I remember that very clearly. The summit, and the woman I loved beside me, and the car I had built out of three thousand bags of nothing, singing its dry high song through the mountains. If I could choose one minute of my life to keep, I would keep one of those minutes. I would not even need to know which.
Then there was a curve.
I don’t remember the curve itself. I remember the headlights sweeping across a wall of rock, and then sweeping across nothing, and then nothing.

I woke in a hospital in Pasadena. My left wrist was broken in two places. There was a long bruise across my chest from the seat belt, going from my left shoulder down to my right hip, like a sash. My face was cut. A doctor told me that I had been very lucky.

He told me other things too. He said them gently and slowly and more than once. I don’t remember the words. I remember the shape of the room while he said them, and a television in the corner with the sound off, showing the weather.
Later the doctor came back alone to look at my wrist. He turned it over in his hands and studied the X-ray against the window.
“This kind of break,” he said, not really to me. “You usually see it when someone’s holding on to something hard. Bracing.”
I said I must have been holding the door handle.
He nodded and wrote something down.
A highway patrol officer came the next afternoon. He was young and polite and he sat on the visitor’s chair with his hat on his knees, and he asked me what I remembered.
I told him. I told him she had wanted to drive it first. I told him about the keys in her hand, and her laughing at the low seat, and her arm out of the window in the cold.
He listened. He wrote something in his notebook. He did not look at me while he wrote it. Then he thanked me and stood up and put his hat on and said he was very sorry for my loss.
My mother was standing at the window. She did not turn around the whole time he was there.
That was the last season Roxana wrote on the calendar.

When I came home from the hospital a week later, with my arm in a cast and my mother holding the door, I went into the kitchen and looked at it. THE CAR, in red marker, and the little drawing of the car with the question mark in the driver’s seat.
There was no line across the bottom of the month. There was no Welcome back.
There was nobody left to write it.
Tales of the Wanting · I The Valley of Diamonds
This is an old story. It is told in The Thousand and One Nights, in the second voyage of the sailor Sindbad, and it is older than the book that holds it.

Sindbad was a merchant of Baghdad who could not stay home. Every time he made his fortune he swore he would never go to sea again, and every time, within a year, the wanting came back, and he went down to the harbour and found a ship.

On his second voyage he fell asleep on an island and woke to find the ship gone without him. He wandered until he came to the edge of a great valley with walls so steep no man could climb them. The floor of the valley glittered. It was covered in diamonds, more than he had ever seen, more than any king had ever owned, lying loose on the ground like gravel after rain. And among the diamonds, sleeping in the heat, lay serpents as long as palm trees.
No man could go down into that valley and come out again. But the merchants of the country had found a way.

They would kill a sheep, skin it, and throw the raw meat from the top of the cliff. It fell among the diamonds, and the wet meat picked them up, the way bread picks up crumbs. Then the great eagles of the mountains would see the meat, and dive, and carry it up to their nests on the cliff top to eat. And the merchants would rush at the nests, shouting and banging pots, and the frightened eagles would fly off, and the merchants would pick the diamonds out of the meat.
That is how diamonds were harvested in that country. By feeding something hungry. By waiting for the hunger to lift the stones out of a place no person could reach.

Sindbad watched this. And then Sindbad did a thing no merchant had ever thought of. He filled his pockets and his belt and his turban with the largest diamonds he could find. He took a piece of the thrown meat and tied it to his own back with his sash. And he lay down on the floor of the valley among the serpents, and he waited.
An eagle came. It took the meat in its claws, and the man with it, and carried them both up out of the valley.
The story says he became the richest man in Baghdad. The story says he went home and swore, again, never to go to sea.
The story does not say how it felt to lie very still among the serpents, tied to the meat, waiting to be taken by something hungry, and to call that a plan.
II. PLANNING
The Retort
Roxana had never wanted a grave.

She told me so once, years before, when we drove past a cemetery in the Valley with rows of flat bronze plaques set into the lawn like tiles. “All that grass,” she said, “and nobody can sit on it.” She said she wanted to be burned and given back to the sea. I said mm. I was in a season. It is in the same part of my mind as the beach at Zuma, the part where things go in and do not come out.

Her parents had raised her without religion. Mine had not, and in the faith my mother grew up in, the body is washed and wrapped and buried in the ground before the next sunset, and it is never burned. My mother said nothing about it. She went into the bathroom and ran the tap so we would not hear her, and came out with her face washed, and said that Roxana’s wishes were Roxana’s wishes, and that was the end of it.
It was not the end of it for her. I know that now.

The crematorium was in an industrial street in the Valley, between a tyre shop and a company that rented out portable toilets. It was a low building with a car park in front and a small garden of white gravel and one olive tree. You would drive past it a hundred times and never know.

In California the family is allowed to watch. I did not know that until the funeral director asked us, in a quiet room with a box of tissues on every table, whether we would like to be present for what he called the committal. He said some families found it helped. Some found it did not.
I said yes before anybody else could answer.

I want to be honest about why. Some of it was love. Some of it was that I could not bear the idea of her going into a room I was not allowed to see. And some of it, I am sorry to say, was the other thing. I wanted to see how it was done.

There is a window. That is the first thing to understand. The family stands in a small room painted the colour of milky coffee, with a few chairs nobody sits in, and a long window in one wall, and on the other side of the window is the machine.

It is called a retort. I learned that word that morning and I have not been able to forget it. It is a word from old chemistry, for the glass vessel an alchemist heated over a flame. This one was not glass. It was a steel box the size of a small car, lined inside with firebrick, with a heavy door at one end that lifted straight up like a guillotine. It was painted a dull cream, and someone had stuck a small plastic plant on the top of it, and I thought about that plant for a long time afterwards. Someone who worked there every day had thought the machine looked lonely.

Roxana came in on a steel trolley. She was not in a coffin. She was in a plain box of thick cardboard, because she had said once, laughing, that it was a crime to burn good wood. Her name was written on the end of it in black marker, in capital letters, in a stranger’s hand.
My mother made a small sound when she saw the marker.

The operator was a big quiet man of about sixty, in a grey work shirt. He looked through the window at us, and nodded once, the way you nod to someone across a room at a funeral. Then he pressed a button, and the door of the retort rose.

I could see the inside. The bricks glowed a deep, dark orange, like the inside of Roxana’s kiln on the second day of a firing. The heat came through the glass. It was not much, but you could feel it on your face, the way you feel a fire in another room.

Sahar was standing in front of Kaveh. She had both her hands over his eyes. He did not fight her. He stood very still with his sister’s hands on his face, and I could see his lips moving under her fingers. He was counting. I knew he was counting. I did not know what.
The operator slid the box in. It went smoothly, on rollers. The door came down.
For a moment nothing happened. Then there was a sound, low and steady, like wind in a chimney, as the burners lit. It went on and on.
I asked the operator, afterwards, how hot it got.

My mother was in the car with the children. I had gone back in alone, saying I had left my sunglasses, and I found him in a corridor behind the window room, drinking coffee from a paper cup. He did not seem surprised to see me. I think he had seen men like me before.
“About sixteen, seventeen hundred,” he said. “Fahrenheit. A bit over nine hundred in Celsius.”
“How long?”
“Two hours. Bit more. Depends on the person.”
“What’s left?”
He looked at me then. Not unkindly. He looked at me the way the jeweller in Beverly Hills had looked at me over the loupe, sixteen years before.

“Bone,” he said. “That’s all that’s left, in the end. The rest goes up the stack. The bone we let cool, and then it goes in a processor, and it comes out like coarse sand. Grey and white. That’s what you get back. Four, five pounds, for a grown woman.”
“Not ash?”
“People call it ash. It’s bone.” He drank his coffee. “Everything soft burns. Everything soft is carbon and water, mostly. It goes up into the air. What you get back is what was holding her up.”
I stood in the corridor and wrote down what he had said in the notes on my phone. Every word. Carbon. Goes up the stack. What was holding her up.

I knew, even then, that this was not normal. I knew a man whose wife had just gone into a furnace should not be standing in a corridor taking notes. I did it anyway. My hand needed something to do. It was the basement again, the exercise book under the pillow, the total at the top of the page. I was making a mark.
When I got back to the car my mother looked at my face, and then at the phone in my hand, and did not ask about the sunglasses.
They gave her back to us four days later in a black plastic box with a label on the lid. Inside was a clear plastic bag, sealed with a metal tie, and inside the bag was Roxana.

The operator had been right. It did not look like ash. It looked like the coarse grey sand at the bottom of a fish tank, with small pale pieces in it, like broken shell. It weighed a little over four pounds. I know because I weighed it on the kitchen scale, the same scale she had used to weigh glaze. Sahar watched me do it from the doorway, and then turned and went upstairs, and I heard her door close very quietly. She had learned from her grandmother how to close a door so that the quiet was louder than a slam.
We put the box on the shelf in the living room, beside the grey-blue bowl. Nobody suggested it. It went there by itself, the way furniture finds its place in a new house.
No Task
Grief, it turns out, has nothing for you to do.

I had expected it to be a kind of work. I thought it would be like dead air, only heavier, and I had lived through dead air a dozen times. I thought I knew its shape. You lie on the floor. You wait. Eventually something catches, and the engine starts, and you are saved.

But grief is not dead air. In dead air the engine has nothing in front of it. In grief, the thing in front of it is a hole, and the engine runs straight into the hole, over and over, all day and all night, because the hole is the only thing there. You keep reaching for a task, and there is no task. There is no problem to solve. There is nothing to learn. She is not hidden somewhere. She is not a puzzle. She is gone, and gone has no moving parts.

I tried. God knows I tried. In the first week I got out eleven books about grief, the same number again, noticed, and stopped at seven. I read the research on how long the worst part lasts. I made a spreadsheet of the paperwork: the death certificate, the bank, the insurance, her studio lease, the gallery that still had nine of her bowls on consignment. I finished the spreadsheet in an afternoon. Then there was nothing left on it.

My wrist was in a cast. I could not work in the garage. I would not have gone in there anyway. The car was gone. The insurance company had taken what was left of it on the back of a truck. The three thousand empty bags were still hanging from the ceiling on their wires, and when the canyon wind came through the side door they turned and clicked against each other. I kept the side door shut.

My mother moved into the spare room. She did not ask. She arrived on the second day with a suitcase and a bag of groceries and her gold tea spoon wrapped in a napkin in her handbag, the way she had carried it out of Tehran, and she simply stayed.

She cooked. She drove Kaveh to school, and picked him up, and sat with him at the kitchen table while he did his homework, which he did very slowly and very neatly, rubbing out any letter that was not perfect until he wore holes in the paper. She did the laundry. She sorted Roxana’s clothes into three piles on the bed: for the family, for charity, for later. She left the third pile alone.
She watched me. She did not say much. She had her basement face on, all day, every day.

Sahar went back to school after a week. She went because she wanted to be out of the house, and I understood that, and did not stop her. She came home and went to her room. She ate dinner with us and talked to her grandmother and to her brother, and answered me when I spoke to her, politely, in short sentences, the way you answer a teacher you do not like.
I knew something was wrong between us. I could not see what it was. I put it in the part of my mind where things go to wait for the end of a season.
Roxana came back on the ninth day.

I was in the kitchen at about two in the morning, because I could not sleep and I did not want to lie in our bed. I was standing at the counter with a glass of water, looking at nothing. And I heard the kiln door.

You need to know that sound. Her kiln was in a shed at the bottom of the garden. It had a heavy steel door with a latch, and when you opened it the hinges made a long dry squeal, two notes, high and then low, like a bird. I had heard that sound perhaps three thousand times in sixteen years. You do not mistake it.
I heard it. High and then low. Then the latch.

I went out into the garden in my bare feet. It was cold and the grass was wet. The shed was dark and the door was closed and padlocked, the way my mother had left it. The kiln was cold. I put my hand on it to be sure.
I stood there for a long time.

Then I went back to the house, and as I came in through the kitchen door I saw her. She was standing at the counter where I had been standing, with her back to me, in my old university sweatshirt, with her hair tied up with a pencil. She was looking down at something in her hands. A bowl, I think.
I said her name.
She was not there. There was the counter, and the glass of water I had left on it, and the light over the stove.
I want to tell you that I thought I was going mad. I did not. I did what I always do. I looked it up.

It is very common. That is the first thing I learned. Doctors call it a grief hallucination, or sometimes a sense of presence, and some studies say that half of all people who lose someone they love will see them, or hear them, or smell them, or feel them sit down on the edge of the bed, at least once in the months afterwards. For people who lose a husband or a wife, it may be more than half. It is not a sign that something is broken. It is the mind doing what it has always done. For years the mind has expected that person to be there, at that counter, at that hour. It has drawn them in so many times that it goes on drawing them, out of habit, after they are gone.
I read that sentence many times. It goes on drawing them, out of habit.

It made sense to me. It was the engine. My mind had studied Roxana for sixteen years the way it studied everything, and it had built a model of her so complete that the model went on running by itself.

She came back four more times that month. Twice I heard the kiln. Once I smelled the clay on her hands, wet and mineral, like a riverbank, as I was falling asleep. Once, the strangest, I was sitting in the dark living room in front of the shelf with the black box on it, and I felt her sit down on the arm of the sofa beside me, the way she always did, and I felt the sofa tilt under her weight.
I did not look. I knew if I looked she would be gone. So I sat still, and she sat still, and after a while the sofa came level again.
I did not tell anyone. Not my mother. Not Sahar.
I see now that I should have told Sahar. I think she was hearing the kiln too.
On the twenty-third night I found the thing that saved me. That is how I thought of it then. I want to keep the word, because it is what I believed, and this book is about what I believed.

I was at the kitchen table with my laptop at three in the morning, reading, as I did every night, about anything that would hold still long enough to be read. I had gone from grief to cremation, from cremation to the chemistry of bone, from bone to carbon. It was the operator’s word, still sitting in my phone. Carbon. Goes up the stack.
And from carbon, in the way that one link leads to the next at three in the morning, I came to a page about diamonds.
I sat up.
There are companies, it said, that can make a diamond from a person.
I will tell you how it works, because I learned it that night and I have never stopped knowing it.

A diamond is carbon. Nothing else. The same element as the lead in a pencil and the soot in a chimney, only with the atoms packed into a different shape, a tight three-dimensional lattice, each atom locked to four others, which is why a diamond is the hardest natural thing we know. In the earth, diamonds form about a hundred and fifty kilometres down, under heat and a pressure we can barely imagine, over hundreds of millions of years. Then a kind of volcanic eruption from very deep brings a few of them up to the surface, in pipes of rock.

But you do not need a hundred million years. Since the 1950s, people have been able to make diamonds in a machine. You take pure carbon, put it in a press with a tiny seed crystal of diamond, and squeeze it at the pressure of the deep earth and the heat of a furnace. The machine is called an HPHT press: high pressure, high temperature. The carbon crystallises onto the seed, atom by atom, and in a few weeks you have a stone. It is not an imitation. It is a real diamond, harder than anything, carbon in its tightest shape. It simply did not come out of the ground.
And the carbon can come from anywhere. From graphite. From sugar. From a lock of hair.
From what is left of a person.

The laboratory takes some of the remains, a pound or so, and draws out the carbon with acids and heat, and purifies it again and again until it is almost nothing but carbon. They turn it into graphite. They put the graphite in the press with a seed. A few weeks later, or a few months, they send you a diamond.

I read the pages of every laboratory I could find. There were not many. Two in Europe, one in America, a few others. I read the whole of every site. I read the reviews. I read the forums where people talked about the stones they had received, and showed photographs: small stones, most of them, on rings and pendants, and many of them blue.

Blue, the pages said, because of boron. A trace of the element boron stays with the carbon however clean you make it, and boron turns a diamond blue. The more boron, the deeper the blue. Every person’s stone is a different shade. Some come out almost colourless. Some come out yellow, where the carbon picked up nitrogen in the press. No two are the same. Like the person, one page said, which made me angry, because it was a sentence written to sell something, and it was also true.
I looked at the grey-blue bowl on the shelf beside the black box.
I thought of the white feather frozen inside her diamond, sixteen years ago, under the jeweller’s loupe.
I felt it catch.
I want to describe the hook properly, because this is the one that took everything.

It was not a decision. It never is. It felt like warm water poured into a cold room. My back straightened. My breathing changed. The kitchen, which had been grey for twenty-three days, came into focus as if someone had wiped a window. The sound in my head, the engine running and running into the hole, changed its note. It had something in front of it.
It was three in the morning. I made coffee. I started a new spreadsheet.

I did not go to bed that night. In the morning my mother came downstairs in her dressing gown and found me at the table with four browser windows open and a page of notes in my handwriting, and she stopped in the doorway.
I looked up at her. I smiled. I had not smiled in twenty-three days.
I watched her face as she saw the smile. I will never forget it. It was not relief. It was the face of a woman in a basement in Tehran who hears the siren start.
The Spoon
There was a choice to make, on the laboratory’s form, and I made it without telling anyone.

You could have the diamond cut and polished by the laboratory and set in a ring or a pendant. Most people did. Or you could have it sent to you rough, the way it came out of the press, uncut, a small cloudy crystal like a piece of sea glass. Almost nobody chose that.
There was a note beside the box that said: For customers who wish to use their own cutter.
I ticked it.

I did not yet know why. I told myself I would find the best cutter in the world and pay him whatever he asked. I told myself that a stone this important should not be cut by a stranger in a factory in a hurry. All of that was true. But under it, at the bottom of my mind, the engine had already decided something, and it was waiting for me to catch up.

They needed a pound of her. The form said a minimum of 500 grams. They sent a small, heavy, padded box with a sealed jar inside it, and a printed sheet of instructions, and a pair of thin white gloves.
I did it on a Tuesday, in the middle of the day. My mother had taken Kaveh to the dentist. Sahar was at school.

I have thought about why I chose a day when the house was empty. I told myself it was because I did not want the children to see something upsetting. That was a lie, and I knew it was a lie even as I told it. I chose a day when the house was empty because I knew that if anyone saw me, they would stop me.

I took the black box down from the shelf and put it on the kitchen counter. I cut the metal tie on the bag with my mother’s kitchen scissors. I looked for something to measure with. The measuring spoons were in the drawer, but there was something on the counter closer to my hand, and I picked it up without thinking.

It was my mother’s gold tea spoon. She had polished it that morning and left it on a folded napkin by the kettle, the way she did every day in that house, because it was the one thing from her own mother she could hold.
I used it.

I put the jar on the kitchen scale, and I spooned Roxana into the jar, and I watched the numbers climb. A hundred grams. Two hundred. The small pale pieces of bone made a faint dry sound against the glass. I did not stop at five hundred. I thought: more carbon, better stone. I stopped at a little over nine hundred, which was close to half of her. I sealed the jar. I put it in the padded box. I resealed the bag and put it back in the black box and put the black box back on the shelf beside the grey-blue bowl.
It looked exactly the same. That is what I told myself. It looked exactly the same.

I drove the padded box to the shipping office in the town at the bottom of the canyon and sent it by courier, insured, signature required. When I came back the house was still empty. The spoon was on the counter by the kettle, on its napkin, where I had put it down.
There was grey on it.

I saw that. I did not wash it. I do not know why I did not wash it. I think the engine had already moved on to the next thing, the tracking number, the delivery date, and the spoon was behind me, in the place where things go in and do not come out.
My mother found it that evening.

She picked it up from the napkin to stir her tea, and stopped, and turned it to the light over the stove. I was at the kitchen table with my laptop. I did not look up. I felt her looking at me across the kitchen for a long time.
“Kian,” she said.
“Mm.”
“Kian. What have you done?”

I told her. I told her about the laboratory and the press and the carbon. I told her it would be a diamond, a real one, and that Roxana would never be in a box on a shelf again, she would be something you could hold up to the light. I was excited. I could hear how excited I was. I talked for perhaps ten minutes and she did not interrupt me once.
When I stopped, she put the spoon down on the counter. She did not wash it either.
“Sahar wants to take her to the sea,” she said. “At forty days. The chehelom [che-he-LOM].”

The chehelom is the fortieth day after a death. In Persian families there is a gathering then, food and prayers and a visit to the grave, and it is the end of the first and hardest part of mourning. Roxana had no grave. Sahar had decided, on her own, that the fortieth day would be the day they took her mother to Zuma.
“She has asked you three times,” my mother said. “You said later every time.”
I did not remember her asking. I believe that she did. I believe it now absolutely. But at the time I could not find it anywhere in my mind.
“There is plenty left for the sea,” I said.

My mother looked at me. Then she said something I did not hear. I mean that exactly. Her lips moved, and she said a sentence, quietly, in Persian, and I was looking at the tracking page on the laptop to see whether the courier had collected the box, and the sentence went past me like a car on the road below the house.
I have tried for a long time to remember what she said. I cannot. I asked her, much later, and she would not tell me.
She went up to bed without her tea.
Sahar came home late that night. I heard her go into the living room. I heard her stop. Then I heard her go upstairs.

She did not come into the kitchen. She did not say anything. The next morning she came down for breakfast with her face washed and her hair tied back very tight, and she ate her cereal and talked to Kaveh about a film, and when I said good morning she said good morning.
I see now that she knew. I thought, at the time, that she had not noticed. A box on a shelf looks exactly the same.
But you cannot tell the weight of a thing by looking at it. You can only tell by holding it.
Bring Nothing
The stone would take about six months to grow. The laboratory said so in the confirmation email: Your diamond will be ready in approximately twenty-four to twenty-six weeks.
Twenty-six weeks was a long time for the engine to have nothing in front of it. So it put something there.
I needed a cutter. That was the first question. The second came right behind it, the way the second move in chess is already inside the first: why did I need someone else?

I began, as I always begin, with reading. I read about cutting the way I had once read the dictionary: from the beginning, everything, without skipping. I learned that the cutting of diamonds has been centred for five hundred years on one small city in Belgium. Antwerp. That for most of the twentieth century the greater part of the world’s rough diamonds passed through a few streets beside its railway station. That the families who cut there had passed the trade from father to son for generations, Jewish families first, then Armenian and Indian and Lebanese, and that the best of the old masters could look at a rough stone for a week before touching it.

I learned that most cutting today is done in India, in large factories, by young men working long shifts with machines that plan the cuts by laser and computer. That the old hand-cutting of Antwerp was dying. That there were perhaps a few dozen men left in the city who still cut by eye and hand the way it was done in 1919, and that most of them were old, and that almost none of them took apprentices.
I read for a week. Then I wrote to them.

I found the names of thirty-one hand-cutters in Antwerp, from trade lists and old newspaper articles and the websites of small workshops. I wrote to all of them. I wrote the same letter, honestly, in plain English. I said that my wife had died. I said that a diamond was being made from her. I said that I wanted to learn to cut it myself, with my own hands, and that I would pay anything and work any hours and was not afraid of how long it took.

Twenty-two of them did not answer. Seven answered politely, and said no. One of the seven said, quite kindly, that it took seven years to make a cutter and that a man of forty-four with a broken wrist should find a good craftsman and spend the money on his children. Another of them wrote back a single line in Dutch, which I ran through a translator: This is not a hobby.
I read that line many times. It was the first thing anybody had said to me in a month that I completely agreed with.
The thirty-first letter was answered on the twenty-sixth day.

The email came from an address that was nothing but initials and numbers. There was no signature. There was no greeting. There was only an address in the diamond quarter, a floor number, and four words.
Come. Bring nothing. E.

I printed it. I do not know why. I printed it on the printer in my study and sat with the sheet of paper in my hands at the kitchen table, under the light over the stove, and read the four words perhaps a hundred times.

Then I searched for him. It was not hard. His name was Elias Karam [eh-LEE-as KA-ram]. He was about eighty. There was almost nothing about him online, which was its own kind of fact. An old trade directory listed him as a cutter and a dealer. An article from 1985 in a Belgian newspaper, about the last hand-cutters of Antwerp, had a photograph of a thin, dark man with a loupe on a cord around his neck, bent over a wheel, and one line under it: Elias Karam, born in Sierra Leone to a Lebanese family, cutting a stone he has studied for eleven days.
Eleven days. I looked at the photograph for a long time. It was the face. My father’s face over a carpet. My face, I suppose, over anything.
I wrote back that night and asked when I should come.
He did not answer. I wrote again. He did not answer that either. I understood eventually that he had already answered. Come was not the first half of a conversation. It was the whole of it.
I left in the middle of winter, in the month the Persian calendar calls Dey [DAY], a little over four months after the accident.

I told my mother first. She was folding laundry in the spare room, and she went on folding it while I talked, sheet after sheet, the corners exactly matched. When I had finished she held one towel against her chest for a moment and did not fold it.
“How long?” she said.
“Until it’s finished.”
“That is not a length of time, Kian. That is a season.”
I said nothing. She was right. She put the towel down on the pile, unfolded.

“I will stay with them,” she said. “Of course I will stay. Where else would I be?” She looked at me. “But you should know what you are doing. You should say it out loud once. You are leaving your children four months after their mother died, to go and polish a stone.”
“I’m going to make something out of her,” I said. “So they will have her. So she doesn’t just—“ I didn’t know how to finish. “Disappear.”
My mother picked the towel back up and folded it, very carefully, into thirds.
“They have her,” she said. “They are trying to give her back.”
I told the children at dinner.

Kaveh asked how far Belgium was. I told him: nine thousand kilometres, a little more, eleven hours in a plane. He asked how many days I would be gone. I told him I didn’t know. He thought about that very seriously, with his fork in the air, and then went on eating.

Sahar didn’t ask anything. She listened, and she ate, and when I had finished she put her fork down on her plate, very precisely, at the angle that means finished in a restaurant, and she said, “May I be excused?” She had never asked to be excused from a table in her life. I said yes. She went upstairs.
I sat at the table. My mother cleared the plates. Kaveh stayed and watched me.
“Baba,” he said. “Is it a season?”
I looked at him. Nine years old, with his hair sticking up at the back where he had slept on it, and his mother’s eyes, and my engine.
“Yes,” I said. “I think it is.”
He nodded, as if that settled something. Then he got down from his chair and went to the fridge and looked at the calendar for a while. It was still on the month of the car. Nobody had turned it.

I left early in the morning, in the dark. My mother drove me to the airport. The children were asleep. Or Kaveh was. I went into his room and he was asleep on his back with his mouth open and a red Lego brick in his fist, and I stood over him for a minute and did not wake him.

Sahar’s door was shut. There was light under it. I stood outside it with my hand raised to knock. I could hear nothing at all on the other side, not a phone, not music, nothing, which meant she was awake and listening to me stand there.
