I did not knock. I told myself it would be kinder not to.

I had left my laptop open on the kitchen table, with the email on the screen. Come. Bring nothing. E. I did not notice until I was at the airport. I thought nothing of it. I thought, my mother will close it.
Three days later my mother sent me a photograph of the fridge. She did not write anything with it.

The car calendar was gone. In its place was a single sheet of paper from a school exercise book, taped up with too much tape, the way a nine-year-old tapes things. On it, in pencil, in Kaveh’s careful handwriting that rubbed out every imperfect letter, he had drawn a grid of squares. Seven across. Many rows down. At the top it said, in capitals: BABA.
The first three squares had crosses in them.
There was no number at the bottom of the grid. He had not written an end date. He did not know one. He had simply drawn squares, and kept drawing them, all the way to the bottom edge of the paper.
The Diamond Quarter
Antwerp in winter is grey in a way Los Angeles cannot imagine. Not the grey of fog, which moves. The grey of stone that has been wet for five hundred years.

I came out of the central station into a fine, steady rain that did not seem to fall so much as hang in the air. The station is enormous, a cathedral of iron and glass and marble built for a king, and I stood under its great dome for some minutes with my one bag, looking up. I had brought almost nothing. Two changes of clothes. A coat. My phone. My passport. The photograph of the old newspaper page, printed and folded in my wallet.
Bring nothing. I had taken him at his word.
The diamond quarter begins about a hundred metres from the station doors.

You would not know it was there. That is the first thing. It is three or four short streets of ordinary grey office buildings, six or seven storeys high, the kind you see in any European city. But the streets are closed to cars at both ends by steel posts that rise out of the road. There are cameras on every corner, on every lamppost, under the eaves of every building. There are police in a small booth at the corner with automatic weapons slung across their chests, and they watch everyone who walks in.

And the people. Men in long black coats and black hats, with beards and side curls, walking quickly with briefcases chained to their wrists. Indian men in quiet suits, speaking a language I later learned was Gujarati [goo-ja-RAA-tee], from the western coast of India, where much of the trade’s next generation comes from. Older men, Armenian, Lebanese, Russian, Israeli. Almost no women. Almost no one who did not look as if they knew exactly where they were going and what was in their pocket.
It felt like walking into a church where everybody worshipped the same small thing and nobody spoke of it out loud.

The address was a narrow building at the end of the quietest of the streets. There was a steel door with no name on it and a row of buttons with numbers instead of names. I pressed the button for the fourth floor. Nothing happened for a long time. Then the door buzzed and clicked open, and I went in out of the rain.

There was a lift the size of a phone box, and a sign beside it in four languages that said it was out of order, and from the faded look of the sign it had been out of order for some years. I climbed four floors of narrow stairs. My wrist, newly out of its cast, ached in the cold. On the fourth floor there was a second steel door, and a camera above it, and a small grey button.
Before I could press it, the door opened.

He was smaller than I had imagined. That was the first thing. He was a thin, upright, dark-skinned old man, a little shorter than me, in a white shirt buttoned to the collar and grey trousers held up by braces. His hair was white and cut very short. His face was lined deeply, the way old wood is lined, but there was nothing soft in it. His eyes were very dark and very still.
Around his neck, on a black cord, was a loupe.

He looked at me for a long time without speaking. Not at my face. At me, the whole of me, from my wet shoes to my hair, the way I have seen a jeweller look at a stone through a window before he picks it up. His eyes stopped once on my left wrist, where the skin was still pale and thin from the cast.
“You held something very hard,” he said.
I did not know what he meant. Then I did, and something cold went down the back of my neck. It was what the doctor in Pasadena had said, almost word for word.
“A door handle,” I said.
He did not reply to that. He stepped back to let me in.
“Elias,” he said.
“Kian.”
“I know.”

The workshop was one long room with a row of tall windows down one side, facing north. A cutter works by north light, I learned later. It is the only light that stays the same all day, with no sun coming into it, no warmth, no shadows that move. On a grey Antwerp morning it filled the room with an even, colourless brightness, like the inside of a cloud.

Under the windows stood three cutting wheels, each on its own heavy iron bench. They were flat iron discs about as wide as a dinner plate, mounted horizontally, like small record players made for a giant. Above each was a heavy arm with a clamp on the end. One wheel was turning, very fast and almost silent, with a sound like breath. The others were still, and covered with clean white cloths.

There was a long table down the middle of the room covered with tools I did not know the names of yet. There were jars of grey paste. There was a kettle and two glasses. There was a small electric heater that did very little. At the far end of the room, set into the wall, was a safe, an old one, painted green, as tall as a man.
And nothing else. No photographs. No certificates on the wall. No chair, except the one at the turning wheel and a single wooden stool beside the table.
He pointed at the stool. I sat. He sat at the wheel. He looked at me for a while longer.
“Thirty-one letters,” he said. “I know. They telephoned each other about you. A man from Los Angeles whose wife is being made into a stone. The whole street laughed for a week.”
“But you answered.”
“I answered.”
“Why?”
He took the loupe from his neck and turned it over in his fingers. It was very old. The brass was worn pale where his thumb had held it for, I suppose, sixty years.

“Because you said you were not afraid of how long it took,” he said. “Every man who writes to me says that. You were the first one who was telling the truth.” He put the loupe down on the bench. “I could see it in the letter. It was a very long letter, and every sentence was the same length.”
I had not noticed that. I went back, later, and looked. He was right.
He did not teach me anything that day. He talked, a little. He made tea in the two glasses, very strong and very sweet, the way my mother makes it, and pushed one across the table.
“What did you bring?” he said.
“Nothing. Like you said.”
“Good. Then you have room.”
He drank his tea. Outside the north windows, the rain went on hanging in the air over the grey roofs.

“You will want to know the first rule,” he said. “Everybody wants the first rule. Here it is. I will say it once, and I will say it again on the last day, and you will understand it on the last day and not before.”
He put his glass down.
“Every stone carries one tension.”
I waited. He let me wait.

“A diamond grows in the dark for a very long time,” he said. “Under weight. And while it grows, the weight presses into it. Not everywhere the same. In one place more than the others. The stone remembers that place. It holds it, like a muscle holds a cramp. You cannot see it. Not with the eye, not with the loupe. But it is there, and it is waiting.” He tapped the bench once, lightly, with one finger. “Find it before you cut. Or it finds you.”
“What happens if it finds you?”

“The stone breaks,” he said. “On the wheel. All at once. Into pieces. Sometimes into dust.” He shrugged. “Then you have nothing, and it was your fault, because the tension was there from the beginning. It was always there. You only had to look.”
I asked him about the safe. I could not help it. It was the only thing in the room that was closed.

He looked at me for a moment, the way my father had looked at me under the table in the bazaar. Then he got up, went to the far wall, and turned the dial on the old green safe, left and right and left, and pulled the heavy door open.

Inside were shelves. On most of them were small folded papers, white, each the size of a playing card, stacked in neat rows. Diamond papers, I learned later. Every stone in the trade travels folded inside one.

But on the top shelf, alone, was a small fold of grey cloth. It was soft and old, like a handkerchief that had been washed a thousand times. Something small was wrapped inside it. He did not touch it. He looked at it, and then at me.
“That is the Kono stone,” he said. “A rough diamond I bought in Sierra Leone in 1999. I have never cut it.”

Kono [KOH-noh] is a district in the far east of Sierra Leone, a small country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa. I knew a little of it from my reading. Its ground holds some of the richest diamond gravels in the world, and in the 1990s a long and terrible civil war was fought over them, and paid for with them.
“Twenty-seven years,” I said. “Why haven’t you cut it?”
He closed the safe. He spun the dial.
“Because I have not found the right hands,” he said.
Then he sat back down at his wheel and did not say anything else for the rest of the day.

I found a room that night, through his directions, three streets from the workshop: a bed, a sink, a radiator that clanked, above a shop that sold kosher wine. From its window I could see the edge of the station roof and the steel posts at the end of the diamond quarter, shining wet under the streetlights.
I lay on the narrow bed and did not sleep. I was not unhappy. That is what I want to tell you, and it is the worst thing I have to tell you in this part of the book.

I lay in a cold room nine thousand kilometres from my children, with my wife’s ashes on a shelf in a house in Topanga and half of her in a press in a laboratory somewhere, waiting to become a stone. And I was not unhappy. The engine was running. It had something in front of it, something enormous and difficult and very old, that would take everything I had. The world had gone quiet and narrow around one thing. Inside that quiet I was safe.
I thought of Kaveh’s grid of squares on the fridge, with three crosses in it.
I thought: I will make it up to them when the season ends.
I put that thought in the place where things go in and do not come out. Then I turned on my side and watched the rain on the window until it got light.
Tales of the Wanting · II The Mountain of Light
There is a diamond in the Tower of London, in a crown, behind thick glass, that has been fought over for seven hundred years. Its name is Persian: Koh-i-Noor [KOH-ee-NOOR], the Mountain of Light.

Nobody knows where it was found. The story says it came out of the riverbeds of southern India, long ago, when India was the only place on earth where diamonds were found at all. The story says it passed from king to king the way a fever passes from hand to hand.

In 1739 a Persian king named Nader Shah [naa-DER SHAAH] crossed the mountains with his army and took the city of Delhi from the Mughal emperor. He emptied the treasury. He took the Peacock Throne. He took everything. But the greatest diamond in the empire could not be found.
Then a woman of the emperor’s household whispered to Nader Shah that the emperor kept it hidden in the folds of his turban.

So Nader Shah held a feast. And at the feast he proposed an old custom, an exchange of turbans between brothers, as a sign of friendship. The emperor could not refuse. They exchanged turbans. And that night, alone in his tent, Nader Shah unwound the cloth, and the stone fell out into his hand, and the story says he cried out, “Koh-i-Noor!” — “Mountain of light!” — and that is how it got its name.

He kept it eight years. Then his own officers murdered him in his tent. His grandson, who was blind, was tortured to tell where the family’s jewels were hidden. The stone went to Afghanistan, to a king whose grandson wore it on his arm, and lost his throne, and fled, and lost the stone. It went to the Sikh ruler of the Punjab, who wore it on his arm, and died. His son was a boy of ten when the British took the Punjab, and they took the stone as part of the peace, and sent it across the sea to Queen Victoria.

There is a saying that travels with the stone. Nobody knows who first said it. “He who owns this diamond will own the world, but will also know all its misfortunes. Only God, or a woman, can wear it in safety.”

In London it disappointed everyone. It had been cut in India long before, in the old way, to keep as much of the stone as possible, and it was large and grey and did not sparkle. So the Queen’s husband brought a master cutter from Amsterdam, and a steam engine was set up to drive the wheel, and for thirty-eight days they ground away at the Mountain of Light to make it shine.
When they were done it weighed little more than half of what it had weighed before. More than eighty carats of it had gone into dust on the wheel.
Everyone agreed it shone better now.
Everyone agreed, too, though not out loud, that it was a little less itself.
The Queen wore it as a brooch. After her, it was only ever set in the crowns of queens, never kings, because of the saying.

It sits in its crown today, behind its glass, and every year millions of people walk slowly past it on a moving walkway that does not let them stop. They look at it for a few seconds each. Some of them want it so badly they can taste it. None of them can say why.
III. SPLITTING
Worthless Stones
On the first morning he gave me a jam jar full of gravel.

That is what it looked like. Small, dull, greyish-brown pebbles, some no bigger than a grain of rice, some as big as a pea, with rough, frosted surfaces like old glass from a beach. There were perhaps two hundred of them. He put the jar down on the long table in front of my stool, unscrewed the lid, and tipped a few out onto a square of black felt.
“Diamonds,” he said.
I picked one up. It was lighter than I expected, and colder. It did not shine. It did not do anything at all.

“Industrial,” he said. “Bad colour, bad shape, full of cracks and dirt. In the trade they call them boart [BORT]. They are crushed into powder for saws and drills and for the paste on the wheel. This jar is worth about as much as a good dinner.” He sat down at his wheel. “You will cut these. All of them. Badly. And when you have ruined every one, I will give you another jar.”
“And her?”
He did not look up. “You will not cut her,” he said. “You will cut a thousand stones that are nobody. Then, perhaps, her.”
That was how the days began, and that was how they went on.

I arrived at eight. He was always there before me. I never once in two years saw him arrive or leave; he was simply there when I came and still there when I went. He made the tea in the two glasses. He handed me the jar. He went to his wheel. We did not speak, most days, until noon.

At noon he ate. Always the same: a piece of flat bread, some white cheese, a handful of olives, an apple cut into exact eighths with a small knife. He ate standing at the north window, looking down into the street. When he had finished he washed his hands at the little sink for a long time, and dried them on a clean towel, and then he would come over to the table and teach me one thing.
One thing a day. Never two.
On the second day he taught me where diamonds come from.

“You think the earth is solid,” he said. “It is not. Under your feet, a long way down, the rock is hot and soft. Not liquid. Soft, like cold honey. It moves, very slowly, the way honey moves when you tip the jar.”

A hundred and fifty kilometres down, he said, the heat is over a thousand degrees and the weight of the rock above presses down harder than anything on the surface could. In that place, if there is carbon, the carbon atoms are crushed together into the tightest shape they can make. That shape is a diamond. Most diamonds in the world grew there, he said, between one billion and three billion years ago. They are older than almost everything alive. Older than the first animals. Older than most of the rock you can see.
“Then they sit,” he said. “For a billion years. In the dark. Under the weight.”
“How do they come up?”

“Very fast.” He almost smiled. “Every so often, deep down, the soft rock melts and boils up toward the surface. It comes up through a crack in the earth faster than a car on a motorway, and it carries everything it touches with it. Pieces of the deep. Diamonds. When it reaches the surface, it explodes. Then it cools and hardens in the shape of the pipe it came up through. A carrot, pointing down into the earth.” He drew it in the air with one finger. “The rock is called kimberlite [KIM-ber-lite], after a town in South Africa where they first dug it out. The pipe can be a kilometre wide at the top. Inside it, scattered like raisins in a cake, are the diamonds.”
“So every diamond came up in an explosion.”

“Every natural diamond. Yes.” He looked at the pebble in my fingers. “It grew for a billion years in silence, and then it came up in an afternoon, screaming. Remember that. It explains a great deal about them.”
On the third day he taught me about weight.

A diamond is weighed in carats [KA-rats]. One carat is a fifth of a gram, he said, about the weight of a single dried seed. The word comes from the seeds of the carob tree, which merchants in the old markets of the Middle East and the Mediterranean once used as weights, because people believed every carob seed weighed exactly the same.
“They do not,” he said. “But people wanted them to. That is the beginning of the diamond trade. A small thing that people agreed to believe.”

On the fourth day he taught me the four Cs, the four qualities a stone is judged by. I knew them already from my diamond season, and I said so. He waited until I had finished, then told me again, as if I had not spoken.

Carat: the weight. Colour: how close the stone is to having none at all, because the best white diamonds are the ones you can see straight through, like water. Clarity: how few flaws are trapped inside it. Cut: the shape, the angles, the finish.

“Three of these the earth gives you,” he said. “You cannot change them. The weight is what the earth gave you. You can only lose it. The colour is the colour. The flaws are inside, and they were put there a billion years ago.” He held up one finger. “Only the cut is yours. Only the cut is a man’s work. A great stone badly cut is a pebble. A modest stone cut well can stop a room.”
“So everything depends on the cutter.”
“No,” he said. “Everything depends on the stone. The cutter only decides whether to listen to it.”
I want to tell you about my hands in those weeks, because they are the first part of me that understood what I had done.

They were useless. That was the first thing I learned. I had always thought of myself as a man with good hands. I had rebuilt an engine. I had ground a telescope mirror to a millionth of an inch. I had tied flies for trout and soldered circuit boards and once, during the bread season, made a loaf that my mother said tasted like Tehran.

None of that meant anything here. The stones were too small, too hard, too slippery. They jumped out of the tweezers. They rolled off the felt and vanished into the cracks of the old floorboards, and I had to get down on my knees with a torch and search. By the end of the first week my fingertips were cut in a dozen places from the sharp edges of broken boart. My left wrist ached from morning to night. I could not hold a loupe steady for more than a minute without my eye watering.

Elias watched all this without comment. Once, when I dropped a stone for the fourth time in an hour and swore, he said, without looking round from his wheel, “Your hands are not slow. Your mind is fast. Wait for your hands.”
I did not understand that for a long time.
What I understood at once was the quiet.

I had expected to miss the noise of my life. The phone, the emails, the arguments, the thousand small demands of being a father, a son, a widower, a man with a house and a bank account and a broken car on the back of a truck somewhere in the Valley. I did not miss any of it. Within a week it was gone. The north light filled the room. The wheel turned with its sound like breathing. The rain hung over the grey roofs. My whole life narrowed down to a square of black felt, a pair of tweezers, and a small dull stone that would not do what I wanted.
I want to describe this narrowing honestly, from the inside, because people who do not have the engine think it must feel like suffering.
It does not. It feels like relief.

It is the relief of a man who has been carrying a heavy bag a long way and is allowed, at last, to put it down. The bag is everything else. Your children. Your mother. Your grief. Your shame. The narrowing does not make those things go away. It puts them in a room, and closes the door, and you can no longer hear them. And in the quiet that is left, there is only the problem in front of you, and the problem is simple, and the problem is hard, and nothing that is simple and hard has ever hurt you.
It is the basement in Tehran. It is the tiles on the floor and the exercise book under the pillow. It is the safest place in the world.

I knew, even then, that it was not a good thing that I felt this way, four months after my wife died, nine thousand kilometres from my children. I knew it the way you know, in a dream, that you are dreaming. It made no difference at all.
The Grain
A diamond has a grain, like wood.
That was the lesson of the sixth week, and it took him a whole afternoon, the only time he ever broke his rule of one thing a day.
“Look,” he said, and he put a stone under the big magnifier on the table and turned on the lamp.

It was a better stone than my boart, a clean pale rough about the size of a chickpea, shaped like two small pyramids stuck together at their bases. He said this was the shape a diamond most wants to grow in. The word for it is octahedron [ok-ta-HEE-dron], which means eight faces. Four sides on the top pyramid, four on the bottom.

“Inside,” he said, “the atoms are stacked in layers. Flat layers, like the pages of a book. The layers run in the same direction as those eight faces. Between the pages, the hold is weaker. Not weak. Nothing about a diamond is weak. But weaker.” He touched one face of the stone with the tip of a fine steel pin, very lightly. “If you strike a diamond along the page, it opens like a book. One blow. Clean. Flat. A mirror on both sides.”
“And if you strike it against the page?”

“Then you have struck the hardest natural thing in the world as hard as you can, with a piece of steel, in the wrong place.” He put the pin down. “You will hurt your hand. You will hurt the stone. Or the stone will break the way it wants to break, and not the way you want, and then it is a different stone.”

The old word in the trade for this is cleaving [KLEE-ving]. It is a strange word. It means to split something apart, and it also means to hold on to something tightly, the way a man cleaves to his wife in the old marriage vows. Elias told me that, almost in passing, and I wrote it down. I did not see then why it would matter.
Splitting a stone, he said, takes a minute. Planning the split takes as long as it takes.
He gave me a stone and a loupe and a notebook and told me to find the grain.

I looked for three days. I turned the stone under the lamp a thousand times. I learned to see the faint lines on its surface, very fine, like the growth rings of a tree, that show which way the layers run. I drew them in the notebook. I drew the stone from six sides. I measured it with a small brass gauge that read to a hundredth of a millimetre. I made a page of calculations. On the fourth morning I showed him where I would split it.
He looked at my drawings for a long time, without speaking, turning the pages. He looked at the stone. Then he closed the notebook and gave it back to me.
“Again,” he said.
“What’s wrong with it?”
“Nothing is wrong with it. You looked at the stone for three days. You looked at your drawings for one.” He pushed the stone back across the felt. “Look at the stone.”
On the ninth day of that stone I found it.

I cannot tell you how. I can tell you only what it was like. I was looking through the loupe, the way I had looked a hundred times, and I was not thinking. For the first time in my life, perhaps, I was not thinking at all. I was simply looking. And the stone turned, very slightly, in the light, and I saw the grain the way you see a face in a crowd. All at once, without searching. It was simply there, running through the stone like the lines in my father’s palm.
I put the loupe down. My hands were shaking.
Elias was at his wheel, with his back to me. He did not turn around.
“Now,” he said.

To split a diamond, you first cut a small groove in its surface, exactly along the grain, using the sharp edge of another diamond, because only a diamond is hard enough to scratch a diamond. This takes an hour. Then you set the stone in a holder of hard wax and lock the holder upright in a small iron cup. You set a thin steel blade into the groove. You hold the blade with your left hand, very lightly. You take a small iron rod in your right hand.
And you strike, once.
There is no second blow. If the first is wrong, the second only finishes what the first broke.

I sat with the blade in the groove and the rod in my hand for, I think, ten minutes. I could feel the stone’s grain through the steel. I could feel my own pulse in my fingertips. I could hear the wheel turning behind me and the rain on the window and, far away, the bell of a tram going round the station square.
Elias did not speak.
I struck.

There was a small, flat sound, like a pebble dropped onto a tile floor. And the stone fell open in the holder, in two pieces, and each piece had a face as flat and bright as a mirror. I picked one up with the tweezers and turned it to the north light, and the light went into it and came back out at me, clean, like water.
I want to tell you what that felt like, because it was the best moment I had had since a night in a garage in Topanga with an engine singing. And because it frightens me now, how good it was.

It was warm water through the whole of my body. It was the twenty-ninth night of the Rubik’s cube, and the last move of the San Diego final, and the first time the trading model made money on its own. It was every summit I had ever reached, folded into one small flat sound. For about a minute I was not a widower. I was not a father who had left his children. I was not a son, or a man who had once had a bruise across his chest the shape of a seat belt. I was a man who had opened a stone along its grain, with one blow, the way it wanted to be opened.
Behind me, Elias turned off his wheel. It was the first time I had ever heard the room without it. The silence was enormous.
He came and stood beside me and looked at the two halves on the felt. He picked one up and looked at it through his loupe. He put it down.
“Good,” he said.
That was all. It was the only time he used that word in my first year.
I went back to my room that night and lay on the narrow bed above the wine shop, and I could not sleep, I was so happy. Then I remembered that I had not called home in four days.

I lay there for a while, deciding whether to call. It was the middle of the afternoon in Los Angeles. Kaveh would be at school. My mother would be at the market, or resting. Sahar would be at school, or would say she was.
I decided I would call in the morning. In the morning, I went to the workshop.
Her
The stone came in the spring.

The laboratory had said twenty-four to twenty-six weeks. It was twenty-five. I knew the date it was due, of course. I had known it since the day I posted the jar. I had a countdown on my phone. I had checked the tracking page every morning before I left my room and every night when I got back to it. On the last week I checked it at the noon break too, standing in the corridor outside the workshop with my phone in my hand while Elias ate his apple at the window.
I had given the laboratory the workshop’s address. Elias had told me to. “Nobody signs for anything at that wine shop,” he said. “Things go missing. Here, there is a camera, a door and me.”
On the morning it was due, he sent me out.

He did it so naturally that I thought nothing of it. He had run out of the olive oil he used to clean the wheel; it had to be a particular kind, from a particular shop on the other side of the river, a forty-minute walk each way. And while I was there, he said, I should stop at the bank on the corner of the main street and change some money for him. He gave me an envelope of notes and a list in his tiny, upright handwriting.
I said that the stone was coming today.
“Then it will be here when you get back,” he said. “Unless you would like to stand in the door all morning like a dog waiting for its master.”

I went. I was gone for nearly three hours. The bank had a queue, and the oil shop was closed until eleven, and I walked along the river in the rain, checking my phone every few minutes. At ten past ten the tracking page changed. Delivered. Signed for: E. KARAM.

I ran the last part of the way back. I am a man of forty-five and I had not run anywhere in years. I ran across the station square with a litre of oil in a paper bag and my heart going like my mother’s against my back in the basement in Tehran.

He was sitting at the long table when I came in. There was no box anywhere. No packaging, no paper, no courier envelope. The table was clean. In the middle of it lay a square of black felt, and in the middle of the felt was a stone.
He did not stand up. He did not say anything as I came in. He looked at me, and then at the stone, and then back at me.
“This is your wife,” he said.
I sat down on the stool. My legs did it without me.

The stone was rough, uncut, the size of a small fingernail, and shaped like a rounded box, its corners worn soft. It was not blue. That was the first thing I noticed, and it went through me like a cold draught. I had expected blue. I had read about blue for six months, the boron, the more boron the deeper the blue. I had imagined the grey-blue of the bowl on the shelf at home, the colour of the sea at Zuma just after sunset.
This stone was yellow. A soft, deep, warm yellow, like honey held up to a window, or the last light on a wall at the end of a summer day.
“It isn’t blue,” I said. My voice sounded strange.
“No,” said Elias.
“The pages said they’re usually blue. From the boron.”

“Usually.” He folded his hands on the table. “Sometimes the carbon takes up nitrogen in the press, from the air, from the metal. Nitrogen makes them yellow. Sometimes a little. Sometimes like this.” He tilted his head at the stone. “Your laboratory will have told you. Somewhere in the small print.”
They had. I remembered it. Some come out yellow, where the carbon picked up nitrogen in the press. I had read it a dozen times and forgotten it, because I had wanted blue.
“It’s warmer,” I said. “Than I thought. She was warm.”
He said nothing.
I picked it up.
I want to tell you about this moment exactly, because later, it was the moment I could not stop going back to.

I did not weigh it. I did not measure it. I did not put it under the magnifier or look at it through the loupe or check it against the laboratory’s certificate or write down anything at all. For the first time in my life, I held something important in my hand and did not measure it.

I just held it. It was cold at first and then, slowly, it was the temperature of my hand. It sat in my palm, very small, very heavy for its size, with the north light coming through it and laying a small soft patch of gold on the lines of my skin.

I closed my hand around it. I bent over the table with my closed hand against my forehead and I wept, for the first time since the hospital in Pasadena. I wept for a long time. I wept the way Kaveh cried when Sahar put the red brick in the wrong tray. It came from somewhere below thinking.
Elias did not touch me. He did not leave. He sat across the table with his hands folded and waited, the way you wait for weather to pass.
When I had finished, he got up and made tea in the two glasses and put one in front of me.
“Put her in the safe,” he said. “You are not ready to look at her. You will not be ready for a long time.”
He opened the old green safe and I put the stone in, in a fresh white paper, on the second shelf.

As I did it, I noticed something. I want to record it here only because I noticed it, and I am trying to put down everything I noticed. On the top shelf the small grey fold of cloth that held the Kono stone was lying a little to the left of where it had been. Perhaps a finger’s width. The cloth was folded the same way, the same soft grey, tucked in at the same corner.

I noticed it, and I put it in the part of my mind where things wait. A man as careful as Elias, I thought, must take it out sometimes. He must look at it at night when I am not there. After twenty-seven years.
He closed the safe and spun the dial.
“Tomorrow,” he said, “you will go back to the jar.”
Breath on a Window
It was perhaps three weeks later that he taught me the lesson about fire.

It was a Thursday. The rain had stopped for the first time in a month, and the north light was clean and cold. I was at the table with my jar of boart. I had cut maybe forty of them by then, badly, and split maybe twenty, and broken ten, and the floor around my stool was a small field of ruined stone.
At noon he ate his apple at the window, and washed his hands for a long time at the sink, and came over to the table.
“Today,” he said, “you will learn what a diamond is.”

He set a small block of white firebrick on the table, the kind used to line kilns. On the brick he put a pair of long steel tongs. Beside them he put a torch, a small one, of the kind jewellers use for soldering, connected by two thin hoses to two steel bottles under the table. One bottle was oxygen. I knew that from the label. The other I did not know.
Then he took a small white paper from his shirt pocket and unfolded it on the felt.

Inside was a stone. A small, rough, pale stone, a little smaller than a pea, almost colourless. It had a faint grey cast in the north light, a little cloudy, like the sea on a dull day. Like the colour, I thought, and the thought came and went in less than a second, of a grey-blue bowl on a shelf, nine thousand kilometres away.
“A lab stone,” he said. “Made in a press, not in the earth. Cheap. Worth nothing. The factories in India make them by the bucket now.” He picked it up with the tongs and held it out to me. “Hold it.”
I took the tongs. The stone sat between their tips.
“What do you know about diamonds?” he said.
“They’re carbon.”
“Yes. What else?”
“They’re the hardest natural thing there is. Only a diamond can cut a diamond. They last forever.”

“Two of those are true,” he said. He lit the torch. It came alive with a soft roar and a cone of flame, blue at the heart, almost invisible at the edges. “Hold the stone in the flame. Not at the tip. Here, where the blue is.”
I held it there.
For a while, nothing happened.
The tongs grew hot in my hand. The stone sat in the blue heart of the flame, and it did not change. I thought perhaps nothing would. A diamond is forever. Everyone knows that.
Then it began to glow.

A dull red first, deep, like the coals of a fire in the last hour of the night. Then orange. It was the colour of the inside of the retort in the Valley, the colour of the firebrick behind the glass. I remember that I thought of the retort, and that I made myself stop thinking of it, because I did not want that colour on this.

Then it turned yellow. Then white. Not the white of a stone. The white of a star. It was so bright I could not look straight at it, and I looked at it anyway, with my eyes watering, holding the tongs as still as I have ever held anything.
And as I watched, it got smaller.

Not cracking. Not breaking. Shrinking. Its edges drew in very slowly, the way the edge of a drop of water draws in on a hot stove. It grew round. It grew smaller. It went on burning, in perfect silence, a tiny white sun in the jaws of the tongs, getting smaller and smaller and smaller.
And then it was gone.
There was nothing between the tips of the tongs. No ash. No smoke that I could see. No black mark on the steel. The flame roared on, blue and empty, where the stone had been.
Elias reached over and turned off the torch.
I sat holding the tongs. Neither of us spoke for a long time.
“Where did it go?” I said at last.

“Into the air,” said Elias. “Into this room. A diamond is carbon. In fire, with enough air, carbon joins the oxygen and becomes a gas, the same gas you breathe out. It does not leave anything behind, because there is nothing in it but carbon. Nothing to leave.” He took the tongs gently out of my hand and laid them on the firebrick. “A Frenchman named Lavoisier [la-VWAH-zee-ay] did this in Paris, two hundred and fifty years ago, with a great glass lens and the sun. He burned a diamond under a glass jar, and tested the air it turned into, and proved what it was made of. Kings had killed for diamonds for a thousand years. He showed them what they had been killing for. Breath.” He paused. “You are breathing some of it now.”
I breathed in. I could not help it.
“So it isn’t forever,” I said.

“Nothing is forever. A diamond only lasts a long time because nobody burns it.” He folded up the white paper it had come in, very small, and put it in his shirt pocket. “You see how simple it is? It does not resist. It does not crack. It does not leave a mark. It goes back to what it was before anybody wanted it.”
He looked at the empty tips of the tongs.
“Like breath on a cold window,” he said.
I said it was beautiful.
I want to put that down plainly, because it was the truth, and because I would give anything now not to have said it. I said: “That was the most beautiful thing I have ever seen.”

Elias did not answer at once. He was not looking at the tongs any more. He was looking at me. He was looking at my face very closely, the way he looked at a stone under the lamp, the way he had looked at me on the first morning in his doorway, from my wet shoes to my hair. He watched my face for a long time.
“Yes,” he said. “It was.”
Then he got up and went back to his wheel, and turned it on, and the room filled again with its sound like breathing, and he did not say anything else that day.

That night in my room above the wine shop I could not stop seeing it. The red, the orange, the white. The tiny sun getting smaller. The empty steel. I lay with my eyes closed and watched it again and again, and every time it was beautiful, and every time, at the very end, at the moment of vanishing, something in my chest closed up like a fist, and I did not know why.
I put it down, I suppose, to the retort. To the colour of the fire. To grief.
I did not put it down to anything else. There was nothing else to put it down to.
Carbon
In the second week of summer I wrote to the laboratory.

I did not have a reason. That is what I told myself. The stone was in the safe, on the second shelf, in its white paper, and I had not looked at it since the day it came. I was still on the jar. I was getting better. I was splitting four stones out of five clean now, and Elias had started me on the wheel, polishing small flat faces onto boart that would never be worth anything. Every day the world was the felt and the stone and the north light, and every day it was enough.
But at night, in my room, the engine wanted something. It always does, at night. It does not want rest. It wants a problem.
So I wrote the laboratory a letter with fourteen questions in it.

I asked how much carbon they had drawn from the remains I had sent. I asked about the purity, the stages of cleaning, the temperature and pressure in the press, the type of seed crystal, the growth time. I asked for the paperwork, the logs of the whole process, everything they had. I numbered the questions. I am not proud of the letter. It is the kind of letter that a man writes to a garage about his car.

They answered in eight days. It was a long, polite, careful email from someone who signed herself as a member of the client care team, and it was the kindest letter I have ever received from a company, and it was, I think, the worst news of my life.
I will put it down plainly, the way she did.

When a body is cremated, she wrote, almost everything that is made of carbon burns away and goes up into the air. What comes back to the family is mostly bone. And bone is mostly not carbon. It is mostly a mineral, calcium and phosphate, the same hard white stuff as teeth. Only a small amount of carbon survives the fire, a few grams in all the remains of a grown person, sometimes less.

From the nine hundred grams I had sent them, she wrote, they had drawn out and purified all the carbon they could. It was a good sample. They were pleased with it. But the amount of carbon in it was small, as it always is. To grow a stone of the size I had ordered, they had done what they do in every case, and what was set out on page four of the agreement I had signed: they had added carbon to it. Pure carbon, graphite, from their own stores, mixed in with hers before it went into the press.

She did not say how much. I asked, in a second email, at three in the morning. She answered the next day. She said that it varied from case to case, but that in a stone of my size, the carbon from the person was usually a meaningful part of the whole, and that many families found comfort in thinking of their stone as made with their loved one, rather than entirely from them.

A meaningful part. I worked it out. Of course I worked it out. I took the figures she had given me and the figures in the research and I made a spreadsheet in my room above the wine shop, at four in the morning, by the light of the laptop. At best, the stone in the safe was perhaps a fifth Roxana. At worst, much less. The rest of it was graphite from a jar on a shelf in a laboratory in a country she had never been to.
I sat on the edge of the bed with the laptop on my knees and the numbers on the screen. Outside the window, the sky over the station roof was beginning to go grey.
I want to tell you what I felt, and I want to be honest, because this is the part of the book where you will begin to be afraid of me.
I did not feel that I had been tricked. I had signed the agreement. It was on page four. I had read page four. I read everything. I had simply not let it in.

What I felt was this. For about a minute, a door opened. I saw, through the door, that I had taken half of my wife out of a box with my mother’s spoon and sent her away, and left my children, and crossed the world, for a stone that was mostly something else. I saw Sahar’s face at breakfast, and her hair tied back too tight. I saw Kaveh’s grid on the fridge. I saw that the stone could not be what I needed it to be. Nothing could.
I saw all of that, clearly, for about a minute.
And then the engine said: a fifth is still her.
It said: a fifth is more than anyone else has.
It said: you have already learned to split the grain. You cannot stop now. You do not know how to polish yet.
And the door closed.

I closed the laptop. I washed my face in the little sink. I put on my coat and went out into the grey street, and walked the three streets to the workshop, and climbed the four floors, and Elias was there, as he was always there, and he made the tea, and he handed me the jar, and I went back to work.

He looked at me once that morning, over his wheel, for a long time. He did not ask me anything. I think he knew what had been in the email. I think he had known, the day the stone came, that sooner or later I would ask the question, and get the answer, and keep going anyway.
I think that was the day he was sure of me.
Calls Home

Los Angeles is nine hours behind Antwerp. When I finished at the workshop at seven in the evening, it was ten in the morning in Topanga. When I woke in my room at six, it was nine at night there, and Kaveh was going to bed.
So the calls were short. They had to be. That is what I told myself.

We did them by video, on my mother’s tablet, propped on the kitchen counter in Topanga against the fruit bowl. Most of the time what I saw was my mother’s face too close to the camera, and behind her the kitchen I had left, the light over the stove, the corner of the fridge.

Kaveh was always there. He would climb up onto the stool by the counter and put his face very close to the screen, so close that I could see only one of his eyes, and tell me things. He told me about school, in great detail, in order, starting from when the bus came. He told me that he had started a collection of bottle tops and had a hundred and nine. He told me about a boy in his class who said that his father was dead, and that Kaveh had said no, he’s in Belgium, and the boy had said that was the same thing, and Kaveh had hit him.
He told me that in a flat voice, as if he were reading it out of a book.

He showed me the grid on the fridge. My mother took the tablet over and held it up so I could see. The single sheet of exercise paper had become two sheets, then three, taped together end to end, running down the side of the fridge toward the floor. Every square had a neat cross in it. There was no number at the bottom. Just squares, and more squares.
“How many is it now?” I asked him.
“A hundred and four,” he said at once. He did not have to look.
Sahar was never there.

She was at school. She was at a friend’s. She was asleep. She was in the shower. She had a headache. Once, my mother turned the tablet toward the stairs and I saw her, for half a second, on her way up, in a sweatshirt that was mine and then had been her mother’s, and I said her name, and she kept walking, and I heard her door close in the quiet way, the way that was louder than a slam.
“Give her time,” my mother said.
I said I would. I said it as if time were something I had a great deal of and was generous with.
I am going to tell you something about those calls that I have never told anyone.
I watched the clock.

Not all the time. Not on purpose. But in every call there was a moment, usually about four or five minutes in, when I would notice that my eyes had gone to the small numbers in the corner of the screen. And with the numbers came a thought, not even in words. It was the feeling you get when someone talks to you during the best part of a film. There was a stone on the felt in the workshop, three streets away, half planned. There was a face I had not finished polishing. There was the north light, which would be gone soon.
My son would be telling me about the bus, in order, from the beginning. And part of me would be at the wheel.
I noticed this. I want to be clear that I noticed it. Every time, I noticed it, and I was ashamed, and I made myself look away from the clock and back at Kaveh’s one enormous eye in the screen.
And every time, a minute later, I looked at the clock again.
Sahar turned sixteen in the spring, in the month the Persian calendar calls Ordibehesht [or-dee-be-HESHT], the second month of spring.

I knew the date. Of course I knew the date. I had it in my phone with three reminders. I sent money. I sent a long message, carefully written, about the day she was born and the window going grey and pink and her fist closed on my collar in the dark kitchen. I asked my mother to make the cake from the recipe Roxana always used, the one with cardamom and rosewater.

I did not call. The day fell on a Tuesday. On that Tuesday I was splitting a stone, a real one, the first clean rough Elias had trusted me with, and the split had to be done in the morning light, and I had been planning it for eleven days.

I told myself I would call that evening. In the evening it was morning in Los Angeles and she was at school. I told myself I would call that night. That night I fell asleep in my clothes on the narrow bed.
She sent me one line, the next day. It was the first message she had sent me since I left.
thanks for the money.
No capital letter. A full stop at the end.
I read it perhaps two hundred times. I wrote a dozen replies and deleted them. In the end I wrote: Happy birthday, sweetheart. I’m sorry I didn’t call. I love you.
She did not answer.

I put the phone face down on the bed, the way I had once put it face down on the workbench in the garage, so that its buzzing would not shake the mirror. And in the morning I went back to the workshop, and Elias made the tea, and handed me the jar.
Here is the worst of it, and then I will stop.

That night, lying awake, I understood perfectly well what I was doing. I could have written it down as clearly as Roxana wrote the seasons on the fridge. THE STONE SEASON. Expected end: unknown. I knew my children were on the other side of a door I had closed. I knew the door was in my own mind and that I was the one holding it shut.
And I thought, quite calmly: I will make it up to them when the season ends.

I had thought it before. In the basement. At sixteen, in the doorway with the trophy. In the garage, every night of the car. I had thought it so many times in my life that it no longer felt like a thought. It felt like a fact.
I did not ask myself what would happen if the season did not end.
I did not ask myself what I would do if, when it ended, there was nobody left on the other side of the door to make it up to.
I turned over on the narrow bed above the wine shop, and listened to the trams going round the station square, and planned tomorrow’s stone.
Tales of the Wanting · III The Cutter Who Waited
They tell this one in the cafés behind the station in Antwerp, late, when the trade is finished for the day and the old men have had their second glass. Nobody knows if it is true. Nobody minds.

There was once a cutter in this city, they say, who was the best of his generation. Kings sent him their stones. When he was young he could look at a rough for a week and see inside it the way a midwife sees a child. When he was old he could do it in a day.
And in his safe he kept one stone that he never cut.

It was the finest rough he had ever held. It had come to him in his middle years, from far away, from a place he never named, and he paid for it a price he never named either. The other cutters knew it was there. Sometimes, late at night, when they passed his window, they saw his lamp lit and his shape at the table, and they knew he had it out, under the glass, and was looking at it.
Year after year, they asked him why he did not cut it.
“Not with these hands,” he said.
They thought he meant his hands were not good enough. They laughed. His hands were the best in the city.
“Then whose?” they said.
“Clean ones,” he said.

Forty years he waited. Apprentices came and went. Some were brilliant. Some were faithful. Some were both. He watched each of them for a year, two years, and then he sent them away, or let them stay and never showed them the stone. The street said he would die with it in his safe, uncut, and be buried with it in his pocket, and good luck to the gravediggers.

Then one winter a young man came to his door, from very far away, who knew nothing. Who had never held a diamond in his life. Who had come for a reason of his own, which had nothing to do with the old man, and which filled him so completely that he hardly saw anything else.
The old man took him on. The street was astonished.

And in the end, they say, it was this boy who cut the stone. Not knowing what it was. The old man simply put it in front of him one morning, among the others, and said, “This one next.” And the boy cut it the way he cut everything that year, as if his life depended on it, because to him, it did. And it came out of his hands more beautiful than anything the city had seen in a generation.
The old men in the cafés always stop here, and drink, and look at each other.
Then somebody always asks the question. Was that fair? To the boy?
And somebody always answers, the same way, in the same words, as if it were the end of a prayer.
“Clean hands are only hands that do not know what they are holding.”
IV. GRINDING
Four in the Morning
He brought her out of the safe at the end of summer.

He did not say anything. He simply came to the table one morning, after the tea, and instead of the jar he put down a white paper, and unfolded it, and there she was on the felt. The soft yellow. The rounded corners. The north light going into her and coming back the colour of honey.
“Plan,” he said. “Only plan. Do not touch her with anything but your eyes.”
I planned her for four months.

Planning, he had taught me, is most of cutting. You look at a rough stone and you decide what is inside it. Not what it is, but what it could become. Every rough holds many possible stones, the way a block of marble holds many possible statues, and only one of them can be cut. To make one, you must grind away all the others. Whatever you take off is gone forever, as dust on the wheel.
“Most of the stone you will throw away,” he said. “Half. Sometimes more. The art is in knowing which half.”

So I looked. I looked at her under the lamp, under the loupe, under the big magnifier, in the north light of morning and the flat grey light of afternoon. I drew her from every side, as I had drawn the boart, but a hundred times more carefully. I found her grain. I found her flaws, small ones, and I gave each of them a name in my notebook, the way an astronomer names stars. I measured her to a hundredth of a millimetre, again and again, until I knew her shape the way I had known the Rubik’s cube: with my eyes closed, all six faces at once.
And as I planned, the hours went.
I began to arrive earlier.

Seven. Then six. Then, by the autumn, four in the morning, walking the three empty streets in the dark under the cameras, past the police booth where a bored young officer would lift two fingers to me from inside the glass. I climbed the four floors in the dark, and pressed the grey button, and the door opened.
He was always there.

I want to put that down plainly, because it began to frighten me a little, and because I never found out how. At four in the morning, at midnight, on a Sunday, on Christmas Day, when the whole city was shut and silent and the steel posts were up at both ends of the street, I pressed the button and the door opened and he was at his wheel in the north window, in his white shirt buttoned to the collar, as if he had been sitting there since the day he was born.
He never asked why I had come so early. He made the tea. He went back to his wheel.

I stopped eating breakfast. Then I stopped eating lunch. I would eat something at night, standing at the sink in my room, bread, cheese, whatever was there, the way Elias ate his apple at the window, as fuel. I lost weight. My trousers slipped. I tightened my belt to the last hole, and then made a new hole with the point of a pair of scissors, and then another.

I slept three hours a night, then two. Sometimes I did not sleep. I would lie on the narrow bed with my eyes closed and see her on the felt, turning slowly under the lamp, and at three I would give up and get dressed and walk to the workshop.
And I was happy.

That is the thing I have to keep saying, because it is the thing no one believes. I was happier than I had been since the night in the garage with the engine singing. My body was falling apart and my children were nine thousand kilometres away and my wife was in a box on a shelf and in a stone on a felt and in neither, and I was happy. The burn does that. It burns away everything that hurts. It burns away everything else, too, and you do not notice, because you are warm.
In the autumn he taught me grinding.

The trade’s word is bruting [BROO-ting], and it is the oldest part of the craft, older than the wheel. It is how a cutter gives a stone its outline, the round shape you see when you look down on a diamond ring from above. You do it by rubbing one diamond against another.

Nothing softer will touch it. Today the big factories in India cut and shape most diamonds with lasers, which burn a line through the stone with heat instead of grinding it. But the old hand-cutters of Antwerp still do it the way it was done for five hundred years, stone against stone. So you set the stone you are shaping in a small spinning holder on a lathe, and you take a second diamond, a rough ugly worthless one, fixed to the end of a long handle, and you press it against the spinning stone. And the two diamonds grind each other. Slowly, with a high thin whine, like a mosquito in your ear, they wear each other down, and a fine grey dust falls from them like ash.

“Only diamond cuts diamond,” Elias said, the first time he showed me. He said it the way you say something everybody knows, like water is wet. It is a saying in the trade, very old, and in Dutch and in Yiddish and in Gujarati they say it the same way.
I wrote it in my notebook. Then I sat with it for a long time.
It is true of grief, I thought. It is true of obsession. Nothing outside it can touch it. Only another one like it can wear it down.
I did not then think about what that meant for the two of us, in that room, at four in the morning, grinding.
Short Sleeves
He told me about Sierra Leone in the winter, a year after I came. It was the only lesson I ever asked for.

It began because I asked. I was at the lathe, and I had stopped for tea, and I asked him where he was born. It was the first personal question I had asked him in a year. He looked at me over his glass for a while.
“Kono,” he said. “You know this.”
“I know the word. I don’t know the place.”

He was silent for so long I thought he would not answer. Then he put his glass down and began to talk, in his flat, even, unhurried voice, the voice he used for the grain and the carats and the four Cs, as if this were simply one more thing about diamonds that I needed to learn. Which, I suppose, it was.

Sierra Leone [see-AIR-ah lee-OHN] is a small country on the west coast of Africa, he said. Green. Very wet. Mountains near the sea, and a great harbour, one of the best in the world, where the British once brought ships full of freed slaves to start a new life. That is where the capital got its name: Freetown.

In the east, far from the sea, in the forest, is Kono. And in the 1930s, a British survey team found that the gravel in the riverbeds of Kono was full of diamonds. Not deep in pipes of rock, the way they are in South Africa. Near the surface. Washed out of the old pipes over millions of years and spread through the rivers and the swamps. A man with a shovel and a sieve could find them. A boy could find them.
“So everybody came,” Elias said.

His grandfather was one of them. The Lebanese had been in Sierra Leone since the end of the nineteenth century, he said, traders, mostly from the villages in the south of Lebanon, who had left home poor and found a country where a man with a shop could make a living. They sold cloth and rice and tins and kerosene. When the diamonds were found, they bought diamonds too. They had the cash and the scales and the connections to Antwerp. By the time Elias was born, in a house behind his father’s shop in the main town of Kono, the Lebanese families bought most of the diamonds that came out of that ground.

“I could weigh a stone before I could read,” he said. “My father put them in my hand, at night, after the shop closed. Feel it. How much? I learned the carats the way other boys learned the names of football players.”
He came to Antwerp at twenty-six, in the 1970s, to learn to cut. He stayed. He did not go back for twenty years.
Then he told me about the war.

In 1991, he said, a rebel army came across the border from Liberia, the country to the east. It called itself the Revolutionary United Front. RUF. It said it was fighting a corrupt government, and the government was corrupt, but that was not what the war was about for long. Within a few years the war was about Kono. Whoever held the diamond fields had money. Whoever had money had guns. The rebels took the fields and dug them with forced labour, men and boys at gunpoint, and smuggled the stones east across the border, where the president of Liberia, a man named Charles Taylor, traded them for weapons and sent the weapons back.
“Diamonds for guns,” Elias said. “Guns for diamonds. A wheel. It turned for eleven years.”

About fifty thousand people died, he said. Perhaps more. Nobody counted properly. Two million were driven from their homes, almost half the country. And the rebels did something else, something that the world remembered when it had forgotten everything else about that war.
They cut off people’s hands.
He said it in exactly the same voice. I want you to know that. He did not lower it. He did not look away. He said they cut off people’s hands the way he said a carat is a fifth of a gram.

They did it to terrify, he said. To stop people voting, in the election of 1996, because you vote with your hand, and a man with no hand cannot vote. They did it to punish villages. They did it, after a while, because they had always done it, and the boys who did it were boys, ten and twelve and fourteen, drugged and given machetes. They did it to men, to women, to old people, to babies.
And they had a question they asked first.
“Short sleeves,” Elias said, “or long sleeves?”
I did not understand.

“Long sleeves,” he said, and he touched his own wrist, very lightly, with two fingers of the other hand. “Short sleeves.” He touched the inside of his elbow. “They asked you to choose. As a joke. Where to cut.”
I put my glass down on the table. My hand was not steady.

I want to stop here for a moment, outside the story, and say plainly that this was real. The war in Sierra Leone lasted from 1991 to 2002. The amputations happened, in their thousands, and the question about sleeves was asked, and survivors have told it, many times, to anyone who would listen. The stones that paid for it came to be called blood diamonds, or conflict diamonds, and a great many of them, Elias said, passed through the few streets beside Antwerp’s railway station, through rooms like the one I was sitting in, and into rings in shop windows around the world.

“The world found out,” Elias said. “Journalists. Films. Reports. It was bad for business. So the trade and the governments came together, in a town called Kimberley in South Africa, the same Kimberley as the rock, and made a promise.”

The Kimberley Process [KIM-ber-lee], it was called. It began in 2003. Every parcel of rough diamonds that crosses a border must travel with a government certificate saying it did not come from a rebel war. A country that will not sign is shut out of the trade.
“And did it work?”
He considered this for a while, honestly, as he considered a stone.

“Partly,” he said. “It made it harder. It also made it cleaner on paper than it is in the ground. The certificate follows the parcel. Not the stone. A parcel is a hundred stones, a thousand, from many mines, mixed. And the promise only speaks of rebels. If a government’s own soldiers do the same thing, with the same machetes, the stones are clean.” He shrugged. “Diamonds are very small. Borders are very long. A stone can walk across a border in a man’s mouth and become a different country’s stone.”
I asked him then. I had to.
“Where were you,” I said. “In those years. In the war.”
He looked at me for a long time across the table, the way he had looked at me on the first morning in his doorway.
“Buying,” he said.
He got up and went back to his wheel and turned it on, and the room filled with its sound like breath, and that was the end of the lesson.

I sat at the lathe with the grey dust on my fingers. I thought about the Kono stone, on the top shelf of the safe, in its soft grey cloth, bought in 1999, the year the rebels burned half of Freetown. I thought about it for perhaps a minute.
Then I put it in the place where things wait, and turned the lathe back on, and went on grinding my wife.
The Wheel
The polishing wheel is called a scaife [SKAYF].

It is a flat, heavy disc of cast iron, about as wide as a dinner plate, mounted flat on a spindle like a record player, and it turns very fast, about three thousand times a minute. It is so well balanced that, spinning at full speed, it seems to stand still, and the only way to know it is moving is the sound, like breathing, and the faint cold wind it makes against your face.

The surface of the iron is scored with tiny lines, too fine to see, and into those lines the cutter rubs a paste of diamond dust and olive oil. That is what the oil from the shop across the river was for. That is the dust that falls from the lathe. Diamond, ground to powder, put back on iron, to grind more diamond. Nothing in the trade is wasted.

To polish a face onto a stone, a facet [FA-set], you lock the stone into a clamp on the end of a heavy arm, and you lower it, very gently, onto the spinning iron at exactly the angle you want. And you hold it there. Five seconds. Ten. Then you lift it, and look at it through the loupe, and lower it again. Hundreds of times for each face. A round stone has fifty-seven of them.

“The wheel does not care,” Elias said, the first time I sat at it. “Remember that. Not about the stone. Not about you. It is turning three thousand times a minute and it cannot stop for anything. If you put your hand on it, it will polish your hand.”
It happened in the second winter, in the month of Dey again, almost exactly a year after I came.

I had been awake for, I think, thirty hours. I had started the first facets on her, the first real ones, the large flat face on the top of a diamond that the trade calls the table, because it is flat like a table and it is where the light comes in. It was going well. It was going better than anything had gone in my life. The face was coming up out of the yellow stone like a window being cleaned, and every time I lifted the arm and looked through the loupe, it was a little clearer, a little more open, and I could see a little further in.
I reached across the wheel to adjust the clamp. I had done it a thousand times. My hand knew the way.
My hand was tired. It went a centimetre too low.

I did not feel it at first. That is what everyone says, and it is true. There was a sound, a short high hiss, like a match being struck. Then there was a spray of something across the white cloth on the next bench. It took me a moment to understand that it was red.
Then I felt it.

I looked down at my left hand. The tip of my first finger was not there. The top of it, from the nail down, had been polished away. It was very clean. Very flat. A small, bright, perfect facet, wet and red, where the end of my finger had been.
I remember thinking, very clearly, very calmly: that’s a good angle.
Then I sat down on the floor.

Elias turned off his wheel. He came over, without hurrying, and knelt beside me, which I had never seen him do. He took my wrist in one hand and lifted it above my head and held it there, firmly, the way you hold the string of a balloon. With his other hand he took a clean white cloth from the bench and folded it into a pad and pressed it hard against the end of my finger.
“Breathe,” he said.
I breathed. The room went bright and then dim and then bright again.
“The stone,” I said.
“The stone is fine,” he said. “You lifted your hand. Your hand knew, even if you did not.” He held the pad tighter. “You have given the wheel something. Now it will leave you alone for a while.”

He took me to the hospital in a taxi. It was a big modern hospital on the edge of the city, and it was nearly midnight, and a tired young doctor with a shaved head cleaned the end of my finger and looked at it under a bright lamp and asked, in good English, what had happened.
I told him. He nodded slowly.
“It’s very clean,” he said. “Usually with machine injuries it’s a mess. This is like a surgeon.”
“It’s a polishing wheel,” I said.
“For what?”
“Diamonds.”

He looked up at me, and then at Elias, who was standing in the doorway in his overcoat, very straight, with his hands folded in front of him. Something in the doctor’s face changed. I think he had grown up in the city. I think he knew what that street was.

He stitched the skin over the end. There was not enough left to save the nail. The tip of my left forefinger would be about the width of a matchstick shorter, for the rest of my life, and numb, and very slightly flat.
“No work for two weeks,” he said.
I was back at the wheel the next morning.
Elias made the tea. He looked at the bandage on my finger, and at my face, and at the clock on the wall, which said a quarter past six.
“Two weeks, the doctor said,” he said.
“I know.”

He nodded, as if that settled something. Then he handed me a thin cotton glove, the kind jewellers wear, with the first finger cut off at the second knuckle. He had cut it himself, that morning, before I came. It fitted perfectly.
“Now your hands have paid something,” he said. “That is good. A cutter who has not paid always thinks the stone belongs to him.”
I called home that weekend. My mother saw the bandage before I could hide it. She put her hand over her mouth.
“What did you do?”
“It’s nothing. A small cut.”
Kaveh pushed his face close to the screen. “Show me,” he said.
I did not want to. He insisted. In the end I held up my hand to the camera and slowly unwound the bandage, and showed him the stitched, flat, strange end of my finger.
He looked at it for a long time, very seriously, his one eye close to the screen.
“It’s shorter,” he said.
“A little.”
“How much?”
“About this much.” I showed him with my other thumb and finger. The width of a matchstick.

He nodded. Then he climbed down off the stool, and I heard him go to the drawer where my mother kept the kitchen things, and come back, and climb up again. He was holding the measuring tape Roxana used for her clay.
“Hold it next to the other one,” he said. “So I can see the difference.”

I held my two hands up to the camera, side by side, and my son, who had been ten for nearly a year, I realised, ten, I had missed it, I had sent money, I had missed it, held a tape measure up to the screen in Topanga and measured, very carefully, with his lips moving, what I had given to the wheel.
Inside the Stone
I want to tell you now about the night I went inside her.

I know what it was. I want to say that first, plainly, so you will not think I am asking you to believe in something. I had slept perhaps four hours in three days. I had spent most of those days with one eye pressed to a loupe, staring into a small field of light that did not change. There is a name for what that does to the mind. Scientists call it the Ganzfeld [GANTS-felt] effect, from the German for whole field. When the eyes see nothing but an even, unchanging field of light for long enough, the brain grows restless for something to look at, and begins to make things up. Shapes. Faces. Places. And a grieving mind, as I have said, goes on drawing the person it has lost, out of habit, long after they are gone.
I know all that. I knew it then. I am not telling you what it was. I am telling you what it was like.

It was perhaps three in the morning. The workshop was dark except for the lamp over the table and the faint grey of the city through the north windows. Elias was at his wheel, at the far end, in the dark, still. I could not hear him breathing. I could not hear the wheel. Perhaps it was off.
I had her in the tweezers under the lamp, with the loupe to my eye, and I was looking through the new table, the clean window I had polished onto her top, down into her.

You must understand what is inside a diamond. Even a fine one. Under a loupe, at ten times, it is not empty. It is full of small things that were trapped in it while it grew, a billion years ago, in the dark, under the weight. The trade has names for them, and the names are beautiful, and I had learned them all.

A feather is a crack, a tiny one, flat and white and frayed at the edges, like a real feather frozen in ice. A cloud is a haze of dots too small to see one by one, like breath on glass. A needle is a long, thin crystal of something else, lying in the diamond like a pin. A pinpoint is a single tiny speck of light, or dark, all alone.
She had all of them. I knew each one. I had named them in my notebook, every one, the way you name stars.
And that night, as I looked, they began to move.
Not much. Slowly. The way the lights of a city move when you look down on it from a plane at night, and the plane is turning, and the whole grid of lights wheels very slowly under you.

The feathers were streets. I could see that now. Long white streets, frayed at the edges, going down into the yellow dark. The clouds were the glow of districts I could not see, beyond the hills, like the orange haze over Los Angeles from the Crest road. The needles were the long straight roads between them. And the pinpoints were windows, single lit windows, in houses far away.
And I went in.

I do not know how else to say it. I was at the table with the loupe to my eye, and I was also walking down one of the white streets, in a soft yellow light like late afternoon, the light on a wall at the end of a summer day. It was very quiet. There was no wind. My footsteps made no sound.
I walked for a long time. Down the feather, along a needle, toward a pinpoint. A window. A lit window, in a small low house at the end of a long road.
She was in the window.

Roxana was standing at a counter, with her back to me, the way she had stood in our kitchen on the ninth night. In my old university sweatshirt. Her hair tied up with a pencil. She was looking down at something in her hands.
I said her name.

She turned round. She was annoyed with me. That was the first thing, and it was so exactly her that I nearly laughed. Not angry. Annoyed, the way she was when I came home at three in the morning from a season and found her waiting up, with clay still drying on her arms.
“You’re doing it again,” she said.
“Doing what?”

“Looking for the crack.” She held up the thing in her hands. It was the grey-blue bowl. She turned it over, the way she had turned it over in the warehouse in Venice, to show me the foot. “There’s one in here too. You’ll never find it. You never do.”
“I’m making you something,” I said. “I’m making you into something that lasts.”
She looked at me with her head on one side. Then she put the bowl down on the counter, very gently, the way she put down everything she had made.
“Kian,” she said. “I told you where I wanted to go.”
“Where?”
“I told you.” She was more annoyed now. “On the beach. You said mm.”
I could not remember. I stood in the soft yellow light in the window of the small house at the end of the white road, and I tried and tried, and I could not find it anywhere.
She looked around the room then. Slowly. At the walls, at the counter, at the window, at the soft yellow light. As if she had only just noticed where she was.
And she said a strange thing. I have thought about it more than anything else she said that night.
“Whose house is this?” she said. “This isn’t my house.”

Then she was gone, and the window was gone, and I was at the table under the lamp with the loupe pressed to my eye so hard it had left a ring of bruise around the socket that lasted a week. My face was wet. The tweezers had slipped. The stone was on the felt, lying on its side, very small and very yellow, with the lamp shining into her new window.
At the far end of the room, in the dark, Elias was sitting at his wheel, turned round on his stool. He was watching me. I do not know how long he had been watching.
“You went in,” he said.
It was not a question.
“I saw her,” I said. “She was in there.”
He was silent for a long time.

“People see many things in stones,” he said at last. “At four in the morning, they see everything. It is the eye, and it is the mind, and it is grief.” He stood up and turned on the light over the sink. “Go home. Sleep. You will not cut well today.”

I went back to my room and slept for fourteen hours, the longest I had slept since Pasadena. When I woke the light was going and I had missed a whole day at the workshop, and the first thing I thought was not of Roxana, or of my children, or of the window in the stone.
It was of what she had said.
This isn’t my house.

I put it down to grief. To the eye and the mind. To the Ganzfeld effect, and four hours of sleep in three days, and to the way a grieving mind goes on drawing the person it has lost, out of habit, and gets the details wrong.
That is what I put it down to. I wrote it down that night, so I would not forget. I have the page still.
Two Obsessives
After that night, he began to talk to me.

Not much. Not every day. But sometimes, late, after the north light had gone and the city outside had turned on its own lights, he would turn off his wheel and make the tea and sit down across the long table from me, and we would talk. Or he would talk, a little, and I would listen.
I think, now, that he was deciding something. At the time I thought he had simply begun to like me.
“You have it too,” I said to him once. “The engine.”
He did not ask what I meant. I had told him, in pieces, over the months. The basement. The cube. The seasons on the fridge.
“Yes,” he said.
“When did it start?”

“In my father’s hand,” he said. “The first stone he put in mine, at night, after the shop closed. I was four or five. Feel it. How much? I felt it. And the whole world went quiet.” He turned his tea glass slowly on the table. “I have been inside that quiet for seventy-five years.”
“Did you ever have seasons? Did it ever move on to something else?”

“No.” He looked almost sorry for me. “That is the difference between us. Your engine is hungry. It eats a thing and moves on and is hungry again. Mine found what it wanted at five years old and never let go.”
He had been married once. He told me that on another night, in the same flat voice.
“For eleven years,” he said. “A good woman. From Beirut. She left me when I was forty.”
“Why?”
“She said I looked at her the way I look at a stone.” He drank his tea. “She meant it as a complaint. I took it as the greatest compliment I knew how to give. That was the problem.”
I laughed. I could not help it. He did not laugh, but something at the corner of his mouth moved.
“Roxana never left,” I said.

“No,” he said. “She studied you instead. She wrote you on the wall of the kitchen. She found a way to live beside it.” He was quiet for a while. “That is very rare. You should know how rare. Most of the people who love men like us are like my wife. They wait, and then they leave, and they are right to leave. The ones who stay,” he said, “pay more.”
“What about dead air?” I asked him one night. “When you finish a stone. When it’s done. The emptiness.”
“I do not have it,” he said.
“Everyone has it. If they have the engine.”
He was silent for so long I thought he would not answer. Then he glanced, very briefly, toward the far end of the room, toward the tall green safe in the wall.
