“I keep one stone uncut,” he said. “That is the answer. As long as there is one stone in front of me that I have not cut, there is always something. The quiet never ends, because the work never ends.” He turned back to me. “A man who finishes everything has nowhere to stand.”

I thought about that for a long time. I thought about the Rubik’s cube, given away to a boy in my class. The chess books returned to the library. The firm, sold. The mirror in its box in the garage, never used. The car, on the back of a truck.
“So you’ll never cut the Kono stone,” I said.
He looked at me. It was the long look. The look from the first morning.
“I will cut it,” he said, “when I am ready to stop.”
On the last of those nights, near the end of the second winter, he said the thing I have kept with me longest.

I had asked him whether he thought it could be cured. The engine. Whether there was a way to turn it off. I told him I had tried, at different times in my life, everything. Therapy. Medicines. Meditation, which I had made into a season, which had made Roxana laugh until she had to sit on the kitchen floor.
He shook his head.

“There is no cure,” he said. “Not for us. The engine is not a disease. It is the shape of the stone. It was pressed into you, in the dark, before you knew you were anything. You cannot polish it out. You will only break.”
“So what do you do?”

“You choose.” He put his glass down. “We never stop wanting, Kian. We only learn to choose what we want. That is all the wisdom there is, for men like us. That is the whole of it. It took me seventy years.”
“What did you choose?”

He did not answer that. He looked at the safe again. Then he looked at the stone on the felt between us, the yellow one, the one I had been planning and grinding for half a year and polishing for two months, the one with my wife inside it. He looked at it for a long time.
“Something I could not finish,” he said.
One Sentence
The call came on a Sunday, in the spring, a year and a quarter after I left.

My mother had called first, on her own, the day before. She did not usually do that. She called me in the middle of the afternoon, which was the middle of my night, and when I answered, half asleep on the narrow bed, she did not say anything for a moment. I could hear her breathing.
“It’s Kaveh,” she said.

He had stopped building, she told me. That had been months ago. He had taken apart every Lego model he owned, the castle, the ship, the space station he had built with his mother the Christmas before the accident, and sorted every piece. He had sorted them first into the ice-cube trays, and then into jars, because there were not enough trays. Glass jars from the kitchen, from the garage, from the neighbours. He had forty-one of them now, lined up along the wall of his room in a row, by colour, from white through the reds and yellows and greens and the three blues to the dark bluish grey and black.
He did not build anything with them. He checked them. Every night, before bed, he went down the row with his lips moving, jar by jar, and checked that every piece was in the right one.
“And if one is wrong,” my mother said, “he screams.”

Not a tantrum, she said. The scream from Nowruz. The scream of pain. If one red brick was in the orange jar, he would scream until he could not breathe, until his face went dark, until he made himself sick on the carpet. Then he would find the brick and move it and check all forty-one jars again from the beginning. It took an hour, sometimes. Then he would go to bed.

“His teacher called me,” my mother said. “He doesn’t talk in class now. At all. He sits and he does the work, perfectly. Every letter. And he doesn’t say anything. The teacher asked me if there had been a death in the family.” She stopped. “I told her yes. She asked me if his father was involved in his care. I didn’t know what to say to her, Kian.”
I lay on the bed in the dark with the phone against my ear. The trams were going round the station square. I could feel my heart.
“I’ll talk to him,” I said.

“He doesn’t need talking to,” she said. “He needs his father in the room. I have watched this before. I watched it in a basement in Tehran with an exercise book. I watched it in Westwood with a dictionary. I know exactly what it is.” Her voice broke, just a little, and then came back. “And I am seventy-two years old, and I cannot do this a second time on my own.”

I booked a flight that night. I want that written down. I sat up on the narrow bed with my laptop and I booked it, Brussels to Los Angeles, the Thursday. I paid for it. I got the confirmation email. I lay back down and looked at the ceiling, and for a few hours I felt clean.
In the morning I went to the workshop.

I had planned to tell Elias. I had planned exactly how. I would finish the morning’s facets, the next two on the lower half of the stone, and then I would tell him at noon, while he ate his apple, that I was going home for two weeks, and that I would come back.
I sat down at the wheel. I locked her into the clamp. I lowered her onto the iron.
And I knew, as soon as the facet touched the wheel, that I could not go.

I want to explain why, in the language of the trade, because it is the only way I can explain it at all. She was at the hardest point. The lower facets were half-cut. Their angles had to meet the upper ones exactly, to a fraction of a degree, or the light would not come back out of her. It would leak away through the bottom of the stone like water through a cracked bowl. I had the angles in my hands now. Not in my notes. In my hands, in the muscles of my fingers and my wrist, from three weeks of work. If I left for two weeks, I would lose them. I would come back and my hands would have forgotten, and I would have to find them again, and I might not.
That is what I told myself. I believed it. It was even true.
It was also the engine. I knew that too. I knew both things at once.
I cancelled the flight at noon, standing in the corridor outside the workshop, while Elias ate his apple at the window. It took four minutes. The airline gave me a credit for a future journey.
On Sunday Sahar called.

Not my mother. Sahar. Her own phone. Her own name on my screen, for the first time since I left. I was at the workshop. It was the middle of the afternoon in Antwerp and the early morning in Topanga, and she must have been awake all night, the way she was always awake at two in the morning, that summer, before.
I answered so fast I nearly dropped the phone.
She did not turn on her camera. The screen was black. I could hear her breathing, and behind it, very faintly, the sound of the canyon wind against the kitchen window.
“Sahar,” I said. “Sweetheart. I’m so glad you—“
“Grandma said you were coming home on Thursday,” she said.
Her voice was very calm. She was sixteen. She sounded much older.
“I was. I am. I mean—“ I stopped. “Something came up. With the stone. I have to finish this part, or—“
She did not let me finish. She said one sentence, very quietly and very clearly, as if she had written it down beforehand and was reading it out.
“She isn’t yours to finish.”
Then she hung up.

I sat at the wheel with the phone in my hand for a long time. The scaife turned in front of me, three thousand times a minute, so fast it seemed to stand still. My wife was in the clamp above it, half-cut, with the north light going into her and coming back the colour of honey.
Elias was at his own wheel at the far end of the room. He had not turned round. But his wheel had stopped. The room was silent except for mine.
I thought about what my daughter had said. I thought about it very hard. I turned it over the way I turned a stone under the lamp. I understood every word of it. I understood exactly what she meant.
And then I lowered the stone back onto the wheel, and went on with the lower facets, because the light was going, and the angles were in my hands, and if I stopped now I might lose them.

I want you to know that I chose it. Not the engine. Not the stone. Not grief. Me. I sat at that wheel with my daughter’s sentence in my ears and my son’s forty-one jars in my mind and my mother’s voice saying I cannot do this a second time on my own, and I made a choice, with my eyes open, the way Elias had said we must.
I chose the stone.
That is the lowest place in this book. I am telling you so you know it was a place, and that I walked there myself.
At the other end of the room, very quietly, Elias turned his wheel back on.
Tales of the Wanting · IV The Boy Who Swallowed the Stone

This is a story they tell in Kono, in the east of Sierra Leone, among the diggers. It is told about a boy, in the last year of the war. It may have happened once. It may have happened to many boys. The diggers do not say.

The boy was twelve, and he dug for the soldiers. They had taken him from his village with the other boys, and given them each a shovel and a sieve, and put them in a long pit by the river, and stood over them with guns. The boys dug the gravel and washed it in the river in round wooden sieves, swirling them the way you swirl rice, and the diamonds, which are heavy, sank to the middle of the sieve. And when a boy found one he had to hold it up in the air and shout, and a soldier would come and take it.

The boys were not allowed to put their hands near their mouths. Not to wipe their faces. Not to cough. A boy who put his hand to his mouth was beaten. A boy who put his hand to his mouth twice was taken away.
One afternoon this boy, swirling his sieve, saw a stone in the middle of the gravel that was bigger than any he had seen. It was the size of a pigeon’s egg, and it was as clear as river water.

He did not hold it up. He did not shout. He did not put his hand to his mouth. He bent down to the sieve, the way you bend to drink from a river, and he put his face to the water, and took the stone into his mouth from the sieve with his lips, like a goat takes a leaf. And he swallowed it.
It went down hard. He thought it would kill him. It did not.
That night, in the hut where they slept, he lay awake with the stone inside him and he could feel it, the diggers say, like a second heart, beating slower than his own.

It took three days to pass through him. He hid it in the dirt floor of the hut. Then he waited for a chance, and in the confusion of a day when the soldiers were drinking, he ran. He ran three days through the forest with the stone in his mouth, and at the end of it he came to a town, and in the town under a mango tree there was a foreign man who bought stones and asked no questions.
The man looked at the stone a long time under his glass. He gave the boy more money than his whole village had seen in a year. The boy took the money and went to look for his mother.

That is the story. But the diggers always add something at the end, the old ones, the ones who have dug the longest. They say that a stone remembers. That it keeps the last thing it was given, the way a diamond keeps a feather in it from a billion years ago. That a stone held in the mouth of a frightened boy for three days keeps something of the boy forever, and that whoever owns it after, all their life, will sometimes taste river water and not know why.
And they say one more thing, and they say it very quietly.
They say that not every stone in Kono was swallowed. That some were paid for in other ways. And that the stones which were paid for in other ways remember those too.
V. POLISHING
Tolkowsky
In the summer of the second year, with the lower facets done and the angles still in my hands, he taught me the mathematics of light.

He did it on paper. It was the only lesson he ever gave me with a pencil. He took a sheet of white card from a drawer, and a ruler, and a small brass protractor so old the numbers had worn off half of it, and he drew a diamond. Not from above, the way you see one in a ring. From the side, cut in half, like a slice through an apple.
It looked like a shallow hat sitting on top of a tall cone pointing down.

“The hat is the crown,” he said. “The flat top of the hat is the table, where you have been working. The cone below is the pavilion. The thin edge where they meet, the brim of the hat, is the girdle. And the point of the cone, at the very bottom,” he touched it with the pencil, “is the culet [KYOO-let].”
He drew a line coming down from above, into the table, like a ray of sunlight.
“Now,” he said. “Where does it go?”
A man named Marcel Tolkowsky worked that out, he told me, in 1919.

He was born here, in Antwerp, in 1899, into a family of cutters, one of the old diamond families of the city. He grew up the way Elias grew up, with stones put into his hand before he could read. But he went to London to study engineering, and while he was there, at about twenty years old, he did a thing no cutter had done before. He sat down with a pencil and the laws of light, and he worked out, with mathematics, exactly what shape a diamond should be cut to send the most light back to your eye.

“Every cutter before him did it by eye,” said Elias. “By feel. By what his father did. Some were geniuses. Most were not. Tolkowsky did the arithmetic. He wrote a small book about it. The whole trade has been arguing with that small book for a hundred years.”
He drew the ray again. It came down through the table. It went into the stone. It hit the steep wall of the pavilion, on one side of the cone.

“Here is the secret,” he said. “When light inside a diamond hits a wall at a steep enough angle, it cannot get out. It bounces back, the way your face bounces back from a dark window at night. Every time. Completely.” He drew the ray bouncing off the wall, across the stone, to the other wall of the cone. “So it hits the other wall. And bounces again.” He drew it. The line went up, out through the crown, toward the top of the page. “And comes back out. Toward your eye.”
“So the shape is a trap.”

“The shape is a trap. If the cone is too shallow, the light hits the walls too flat, and leaks out through the bottom of the stone. If the cone is too deep, the light bounces the wrong way and leaks out the sides. Either way, the stone is dark. Lifeless.” He drew a shallow cone and a deep one, with lines leaking out of them like water from a bad bucket. “Tolkowsky found the angles in between. The pavilion at about forty-one degrees. The crown at about thirty-four. The table a little more than half as wide as the stone. And then light that goes in cannot find any way out except the one you want.”
He put the pencil down.
“That is all a cutter does,” he said. “He traps light. He builds a room with no way out but one, and he puts the light inside, and he waits until it gives up and comes home.”

I looked at the drawing for a long time. I had been doing the angles for months without understanding them. Now I understood them, and I felt it catch, the old warmth, the engine taking hold of a new thing inside the old thing.

I could do this. I could do this perfectly. Here was something that could be calculated, exactly, to the degree, to the fraction of a degree. And then I would never have to guess about her again. She would be right, the way a solved equation is right, forever.
“Three things come back,” Elias said, “when the cut is right. The trade has a name for each of them.”
He wrote them on the card in his small upright hand.
Brilliance: the white light that comes back out of the stone, the brightness.

Fire: the colours. Because a diamond bends each colour of light a little differently, the way a glass prism does, so that white light going in comes out split into red and orange and blue and violet. Small flashes of rainbow. They call it fire.
Scintillation [sin-ti-LAY-shun]: the sparkle. The flicker of light and dark across the face of the stone when it moves, or you move, or the person wearing it breathes.
“Brilliance,” he said, “fire, scintillation. Light, colour, life.” He tapped the three words. “A stone that has all three is a stone that has been listened to.”
I folded the card and put it in my pocket. I have it still. It is soft as cloth now at the folds.
Fifty-Seven

A round diamond, cut the way Tolkowsky worked out, has fifty-seven faces. Thirty-three on the crown, above the girdle. Twenty-four on the pavilion, below. Some cutters add a tiny flat face at the very point of the cone, the culet, and call it fifty-eight. Elias did not.
“A point should be a point,” he said.
I had cut twenty-four of them by midsummer. The pavilion was done. Only the crown was left: the table, which was finished, and thirty-two smaller faces around it.
And it was at about this time that I began to give them names.
I want to explain this, because it was the strangest thing I did in Antwerp and, I think now, the only part of it that was not entirely the engine.

I had been cutting for eighteen months. I had cut the pavilion facet by facet, hundreds of touches on the wheel for each one, and I could not remember any of them. They had all blurred together, into one long day at the wheel, the north light and the sound like breathing and the honey-coloured stone in the clamp. And it came to me one night, lying on the narrow bed above the wine shop, that when she was finished I would not be able to tell one face from another. They would be her. And none of them would be her. They would be fifty-seven pieces of nothing in particular.
So I decided that each of the thirty-two that were left would be for one memory.

One facet, one memory of Roxana. Before I touched the stone to the wheel each morning, I would choose a memory, and hold it in my mind, the whole of it, every detail, for as long as it took to cut that face. And that face would be that day. And when she was finished, I would be able to hold her up to the light and turn her, and know which face was which.

It was a ridiculous idea. I knew that. It was exactly the kind of idea Roxana would have written on the fridge in green marker, with a joke under it. THE MEMORY SEASON. Thirty-two days. Bring tissues.
I did it anyway.

The first was the bowl. The warehouse in Venice, the woman with clay on her arms and a pencil through her hair. It’s good enough. That’s the best thing a bowl can be. I cut that facet in four days. It is on the crown, on the left, if you hold her with the girdle facing you.

The second was the night she asked me what season it was, sitting up in bed with the sketchbook. The third was the calendar on the fridge, the first one, Bring snacks. The fourth was Big Sur, the photograph of the sea with no message.
The fifth was the hospital, the night Sahar was born, when she threw the stopwatch across the room.

I cut them through the summer and into the autumn. The wedding, and the violinist playing flat, and her hand pressing mine twice under the table. The night she closed my laptop on the spreadsheet and said she’s a baby, come and hold her. The bread season. The bees.
By the twentieth I was slowing down. Not my hands. My mind. I had told myself there would be no trouble finding thirty-two memories of a woman I had lived with for sixteen years.
There was trouble.
I want to be honest about this, because it was a terrible thing to discover, and it is the centre of everything I have to tell you.
I had sixteen years with her. And I could not find enough memories.

Not because I had forgotten. Because I had not been there. I would reach for a summer, a Christmas, a birthday, and find nothing, or find a season instead. The summer of the Latin season. What did she do that summer? I did not know. I was learning Latin. The year of the firm, the third year. What was she like that year? What was she making? What did she worry about? I did not know. I was on the couch in the office three nights out of seven, eating the same turkey sandwich.
I had sixteen years of a calendar on the fridge, in her handwriting, describing me. I did not have sixteen years of her.
So I called my mother.
I did not tell her why. I said I wanted to hear about Roxana. My mother was quiet for so long on the line that I thought the call had dropped. Then she began to talk.

She told me that Roxana had called her every week, for sixteen years. Every Sunday. I had not known that. Roxana called her on Sunday afternoons, from the studio, while the kiln was firing, and they talked for an hour about nothing. About recipes. About my father’s knees. About me.

“She called me at the start of every season,” my mother said. “Every one. It’s started again, she would say. He’s gone into the cube again, she called it, because I told her about the cube. And we would talk about how long it might be, and what she would do. She kept a list of my recipes for when you forgot to eat. She asked me what you were like as a boy, so she would know what was coming.”
“You never told me.”

“You never asked.” My mother’s voice was gentle. “Kian, she was not waiting for you. You understand? She was not sitting at home waiting. She had a whole life going on beside you. She made a thousand bowls. She had friends you never met. She taught pottery to children at the library in the canyon on Saturdays, for nine years. Did you know that?”
I did not know that.

I sat on the edge of the narrow bed above the wine shop with the phone against my ear and the north light coming up grey over the station roof, and I listened to my mother tell me about my wife. A woman I did not know. A woman who taught children at the library on Saturday mornings while I was in the garage with a car.
I cut a facet for that. The twenty-first. The library. I had never seen it. I imagined it. It is on the crown, near the back.
Kaveh gave me a memory.
I asked him, on a call, if he would tell me something about his mother that I did not know. He thought about it for a long time, very seriously, with his one eye close to the screen.
“She used to sing in the car,” he said. “When she drove me to school. She sang the same song every day. It was in Persian. She said her grandmother sang it to her.”
“What song?”
He did not know the name. He tried to sing a little of it, in his high flat voice, and stopped, embarrassed. I did not know it. I had never heard her sing it. I had never driven him to school.
I cut a facet for the song. The twenty-sixth. I do not know the words. I cut it anyway.
I asked Sahar.

I wrote to her. A short message, carefully, at four in the morning. I said I was making something, and that I wanted to put into it things I did not know about her mother, and that she knew more than I did, and would she tell me one thing. Just one.
She did not answer for three days. Then she wrote back one line.
No. Those are mine.
By the end of the autumn I had thirty-one facets cut and named.
There was one left.
And I knew what it was. I had known for weeks. I had been saving it. Or avoiding it. I did not know which.

It was the beach at Zuma, the last summer. The sun going down. The children far out in the water, Sahar holding Kaveh flat on the surface the way her mother had once held her. The sea that grey-blue colour that goes almost black, like the bowl. And Roxana on the towel beside me, saying something to the sea.
And me, on my phone, reading about valve springs, saying mm.

That was the last memory. The last facet. I knew it as surely as I had known the grain of the first stone I ever split. And it was the only one of the thirty-two I could not see, because I had not been looking.
Fire
I finished the crown, all but one face, on a grey afternoon at the end of the second autumn.

I took her off the wheel and out of the clamp and cleaned her in a small dish of alcohol, the way Elias had taught me, and dried her on a clean white cloth. Then I took the tweezers and lifted her up, and turned toward the north window.

I had looked at her through the loupe a thousand times as I worked. But that was looking at a part of her. One face, one angle, one flaw. I had not looked at the whole of her, the way you look at a finished thing. I had not let myself.
Now I did.
The light went in through the table.

And it did not come back out the way it went in. It came out changed. That is the only way I can say it. It went into the stone white, plain, the even colourless light of a north window on a grey day in Belgium. And it came back out at me in pieces. In flashes. In small sudden darts of colour, red, then orange, then a blue so pure it hurt, then violet, then gold, dancing across the faces of the crown as I turned her, very slightly, in the tweezers.
Fire.

I had read the word. I had written it on a card. I had understood the mathematics: the light bending, each colour by a different amount, splitting apart inside the stone like a choir breaking into its separate voices. I knew exactly why it was happening.
None of that had prepared me for it.

It was as if the stone were alive. As if there were something inside it, something small and bright, moving from room to room, turning on lights. Every time I moved my hand, a different room lit. Every time I breathed, the colours shifted. She was answering me. She was answering every movement I made with light.
I stood at the north window and held her up and turned her, slowly, and the fire moved in her, and I wept.

Not the way I had wept on the day she came, bent over the table with my closed hand against my forehead. This was quieter. It came up from somewhere very low and simply ran down my face, and I did not wipe it away, and I did not stop turning her.
Elias was at his wheel. He had turned it off.

He came and stood beside me at the window, and looked at the stone in the tweezers for a long time. He did not take her. He did not ask for the loupe. He simply looked, with his own eyes, from a little distance, the way you look at a painting in a gallery.
“Yes,” he said.
I could not speak.
“You listened,” he said. “That is not common. Most men who come to this trade never learn. They cut what they want to see. You cut what was there.”
He was quiet for a moment.
“One more,” he said. “The last face. Then she is finished.”
“I know.”
“Do you know which?”
“Yes.”

He nodded. He looked at the stone a little longer. And then he did a thing he had not done in nearly two years, except to stop my bleeding. He put his hand on my shoulder. Lightly. For a moment. His hand was very thin, and very cold, and I could feel the bones of it through my shirt.
“Take a week,” he said. “Before the last one. Sleep. Eat. Telephone your children. The stone will wait. It has waited a very long time already.”
I did not understand what he meant by that. I thought he was talking about Roxana. About her death. About the two years.
He took his hand away and went back to his wheel and did not turn it on. He sat there, in the grey light, with his hands folded in his lap, looking at nothing.
Clearing the Shelves
I did not take the week. Of course I did not. But I noticed, in the days that followed, that something in the workshop had changed, and it took me some time to understand what it was.
Elias was emptying it.

He did it slowly. Quietly. So gradually that I did not see it at first. A drawer of tools I had never seen him use, gone one morning, the drawer left empty and slightly open. The big magnifier on the end of the long table, gone. The jars of boart, all but my own, gone. The small electric heater that did very little, gone, so that the workshop was colder than ever and I worked in my coat.

Men came. Men I had never seen before, in long black coats or quiet suits, who buzzed at the steel door downstairs and climbed the four floors and sat with Elias at the long table for half an hour, speaking in low voices in Dutch or French or Arabic, while I sat at my wheel and did not listen. Each one left with something. A paper of stones. A tool wrapped in cloth. Once, two of them carried out the second of the three wheels, iron bench and all, down the four flights of stairs, slowly, groaning, while Elias stood at the top and watched them go.
Every man who left shook my hand on the way out. Every one of them looked at me, quickly, the way you look at someone at a funeral when you do not know how they are related to the dead.
He stopped eating.

Not all at once. That was the thing. He still ate at noon, standing at the north window. But the flat bread got smaller. The white cheese went. The olives went. By the end of the first week it was only the apple. He still cut it into exact eighths with the small knife. He ate four of them. Then three. Then he ate one eighth, slowly, looking down into the street, and put the other seven back on the plate, and washed his hands at the sink for a long time.

He was very thin now. I had always thought of him as thin, but it had been the thinness of a man who has no use for anything extra. Now it was the other kind. His white shirt, still buttoned to the collar, stood away from his neck. His wrists, when he reached for the kettle, were like the handles of wooden spoons.
I asked him, finally, on a Thursday, when he put the seven eighths of apple back on the plate.
“Are you ill?”
He looked at me for a long time.
“I am eighty-one,” he said. “That is not an illness. That is a number.”
“You’re not eating.”
“I am eating what I need.”
“You’re giving everything away.”

“I am giving back what was lent.” He dried his hands. “Every tool in this room belonged to someone before me. Every stone that comes through that door belongs to someone after. A cutter owns nothing. He holds things for a while.” He hung the towel on its hook, very straight. “I have held them long enough.”
I did not know what to say. I said, “You told me you would never stop. That you keep one stone uncut, so there’s always something in front of you.”
“Yes.”
“Then why—“
“Because I am almost finished,” he said.
He said it simply, the way he said a carat is a fifth of a gram. Then he went back to his own wheel, by the north window, and sat down, and did not turn it on.
That night I did a thing I had not done in nearly two years. I lay on the narrow bed above the wine shop and I did not think about the stone.
I thought about Elias. About his thin wrists and his white shirt and his seven eighths of apple. About the men in black coats carrying the wheel down the stairs. About I am almost finished.

And I thought, for the first time, about the green safe, and the top shelf, and the soft grey fold of cloth that had sat there for twenty-eight years now. I thought: he is giving away everything else. He has not given that away.
I thought: he said he would cut it when he was ready to stop.
I lay there for a long time with that.
Then I put it in the place where things wait, and planned the last facet.
The Last Facet
I cut it in the middle of Dey. The month that falls in the deep of winter. Two years, almost to the day, from the morning I came out of the central station into the hanging rain with one bag.
It was a small facet. One of the eight little triangles that sit around the edge of the table, the ones the trade calls stars. It should have taken a day. It took six.

I held the memory every hour of every one of those days. The beach at Zuma. The children far out in the water. The sun. The sea going grey-blue, almost black. Roxana beside me on the towel. Her voice, saying something to the sea. Me, on my phone, saying mm.
I tried, as I cut, to hear what she had said.

I could not. I knew the shape of it. I knew it was about the sea, and about Sahar, and about going. But the words had gone into the part of my mind where things go in and do not come out, and they had not come out, and they would not come out now, however long I held the stone to the wheel.
So I cut the facet for the thing I had not heard. It was the only thing I could do.

On the sixth day, at about eleven in the morning, I lifted the arm, and took her out of the clamp, and cleaned her in the alcohol, and dried her on the white cloth, and looked at her through the loupe for the last time.
Fifty-seven faces. Every angle where Tolkowsky had said it should be. The light going in through the table and finding no way out but one, and coming home, in fire.
She was finished.
I want to tell you what that felt like, exactly, because it is the last time in this book I will feel it.

It was warm water through the whole of my body. It was the twenty-ninth night of the cube, and the last move in San Diego, and the engine catching in the garage with the bags spinning on their wires. It was every summit I had ever reached, all of them at once, and this one higher than any of them, because this one had cost more than all of them together. A finger. Two years. A daughter’s voice on a black screen.
I stood at the north window and held her up to the light. The first perfect thing I had ever made with my hands. I held my wife in the tweezers, and she was on fire.
It lasted about four minutes.
Then it was gone. And something else came in behind it.
I knew it at once. I had known it all my life. The silence after a station stops broadcasting. Dead air.

I had thought, somehow, that it would not come this time. That this was different. That this was not a season but the end of seasons, the last thing, the one that would fill the hole for good. I had thought, without ever quite saying it to myself, that when she was finished I would be finished too, and I would be able to stop.
It came within the hour.

I sat at the wheel with her on the white cloth in front of me, finished, perfect, on fire in the north light. And I felt the engine go on running, with nothing in front of it. The hum of it in my chest. The restlessness in my hands. The terrible empty loud quiet.
And then I felt it begin to look for the next thing.

I want to put this down plainly. I want you to see it exactly, because it is the most frightening thing I know about my own mind, and it happened in that room, on that day, with my wife’s stone on the cloth in front of me.
Within the hour, before the warmth was even fully gone, I found myself looking at the green safe in the wall.
At the top shelf. At the grey fold of cloth.
And I thought, quite clearly, not in grief, not in horror, but with the old warm curiosity rising in me like water in a well:
I wonder what the Kono stone looks like inside.
I looked away from the safe. I made myself. I looked down at her on the cloth.
When I looked up, Elias was watching me from his chair by the north window. He had been watching me, I think, the whole time. He had seen where my eyes went. He had seen what was in them.

His face did not change. He looked at me for a long time, the way he had looked at me on the first morning, from my shoes to my hair. Then he nodded, once, very slowly, the way a man nods when a stone does exactly what he knew it would do.
“Wrap her,” he said. “Put her on the table. Go home.”
“It’s eleven in the morning.”
“Go home. Sleep. Eat something.” He paused. “Come tomorrow at eight. Not before. Eight.”
I looked at him.
“I have three things to tell you,” he said. “I will tell you each of them once.”
Tales of the Wanting · V Forever
In the spring of 1947, a young woman named Frances Gerety [GERR-uh-tee] sat up late in her office in Philadelphia, trying to write one sentence.

She was a copywriter at an advertising agency, and her client was the biggest diamond company in the world, a company from South Africa that owned or controlled most of the rough diamonds then being dug out of the earth. The company had a problem. Diamonds were not, in fact, rare. There were a great many of them. What kept them expensive was that the company kept most of them locked away, and released only a few at a time. And that only worked as long as people wanted them, and kept them, and never, ever sold them back.
So the company needed people to believe two things. That love required a diamond. And that a diamond, once bought, should never be let go.

Before the war, an engagement ring with a diamond in it had not been a common thing in America. The agency had spent nine years changing that. They had put diamonds on the hands of film stars. They had sent speakers into high schools to talk to girls about engagement rings. They had planted the idea in newspapers and magazines that a man should spend a month’s wages on a stone, and later, two. It was working. But they still did not have a sentence.
Late that night, tired, about to go home, Frances Gerety wrote four words on a sheet of paper, almost as an afterthought.
A Diamond Is Forever.
She did not think much of it. She said so, later, many times. She thought it was all right. The agency used it the next morning. It has been used every year since.

Half a century later, a famous trade magazine named it the best advertising slogan of the twentieth century. By then it had done exactly what it was meant to do. A planet of people believed that love was a stone. That a stone was forever. That to let it go was to let love go. They bought them, and wore them, and left them to their children, and almost never sold them back.

Frances Gerety never married. She lived in Philadelphia and worked at the agency for more than twenty-five years, writing sentences for the company’s diamonds. Nobody ever gave her one to keep forever.
She died in 1999, the year the rebels burned half of Freetown.

A diamond, as anyone who has ever held one in a flame knows, is not forever. In a hot enough fire, with enough air, it burns. It glows red, then orange, then white. It shrinks. It leaves no ash and no mark. It turns, in a few minutes, into the same gas you breathe out.
The four words have lasted much longer than that.

Tales of the Wanting · VI
The Man Who Bought a Hand

This one is not a folk tale. It has no once-upon-a-time and no moral at the end. It happened, in the spring of 1999, in the east of Sierra Leone, on a road outside the main town of Kono. It is told here plainly, because there is no other way to tell it.

A buyer drove out to that road in a white car. He was a Lebanese man, in his fifties, born in that town, the son and grandson of men who had bought diamonds there. He had come back from Europe for the stones. That year the stones were very cheap, because the war made them cheap, and a man with cash and a car and no questions could buy in a week what would have taken him a year in peacetime.

He had done it before. Many times. He was not a rebel and he did not carry a gun. He was a buyer. He drove out to a place he was told to drive to, and men came out of the trees, and they sat in the shade by the road and showed him stones, and he weighed them on a small brass scale he carried in a wooden box, and he paid in American dollars. Then he drove away. That is what buying was, that year, on that road.

On that day, the man who came out of the trees was a commander. He was very young, perhaps twenty, and he wore a woman’s wig and a pair of mirrored sunglasses, and he was laughing. Behind him were boys with guns, and behind the boys, sitting in the dust at the edge of the road with his hands tied in front of him, was a child. A boy of nine or ten. From a village they had burned that morning.
The commander showed the buyer a stone.

It was the finest rough the buyer had seen in thirty years. The size of a fingernail. Rounded at the corners. The colour of honey held up to a window. He took out his loupe and looked into it, and for a minute, the way it always happened to him with a stone, the road and the trees and the boys with guns went quiet around him, and there was only the light going into the stone and coming back.
He asked the price.

The commander laughed. He said the price was already being paid. He said the buyer had come at a good time. The stone was a gift to him, the commander said, because the buyer was a friend of the revolution, and a friend should be shown what the revolution can do.
Then he turned to the boy in the dust, and called out a question, the question every person in that country had learned to fear.
“Short sleeves, or long sleeves?”
The boy did not answer. He was too frightened to speak.
So the commander turned to the buyer, smiling behind his mirrored glasses, and asked him instead. “You choose,” he said. “Friend. Short, or long?”
The buyer said nothing.

He did not say long. He did not say short. He did not say stop, or no, or I will not buy it, or I will give you everything in the car to let him go. He sat in the shade by the road with the stone in his hand and his loupe in the other, and he said nothing at all.
The commander laughed again. He said a man who will not choose has chosen. He said: “Long.”
It was done in front of the buyer, at the edge of the road, with a machete. It took less time than it takes to tell. The boy made a sound the buyer heard every night for the rest of his life.
Then the commander folded the stone into the buyer’s hand, and closed his fingers over it, and patted them.
The buyer drove away. He did not look in the mirror. He drove back to town and took the next flight to Europe with the stone in his pocket.
He never sold it. He never cut it. He kept it in a safe for twenty-eight years, in a fold of soft grey cloth, and told himself he was waiting for the right hands.

This is not a story about the boy. The boy has his own story, and it is his to tell, and he is alive. This is a story about a man who wanted one thing so much, for one minute, on a road in the shade, that he let the world go quiet around it.
And it is about what the world did, while he was not listening.
Three Things
I came at eight.

It was still dark. It is still dark at eight in Antwerp in the deep of winter. The street was empty. The young officer in the police booth lifted two fingers to me from behind the glass. I climbed the four floors, and pressed the grey button, and the steel door opened, and he was there.

He was not at his wheel. He was sitting at the long table, in his white shirt buttoned to the collar, with his hands flat on the wood in front of him. The workshop was almost empty now. The wheels were gone, except his. The jars were gone. The drawers stood open and bare. The green safe in the wall was open, too, and I could see from the doorway that every shelf was empty.
On the table in front of him, on a square of black felt, was the stone. My stone. Finished, on fire, catching the light of the lamp.
Beside it lay two envelopes. One was old and thick and creased, and its corners were soft from being handled. The other was new and thin.
He did not make tea.
“Sit down, Kian,” he said. “Put the stone on the cloth.”
It was already on the cloth. I sat down on the stool across from him. My hands were shaking and I did not know why.
“I am going to tell you three things,” he said. “I will tell each of them once.”
“The first thing is about carbon.”
He looked at the stone on the felt, not at me.

“Carbon does not remember. It was a tree once, and then coal, and then a woman, and then a stone, and it never knew it was any of them. We are the ones who remember. We put the people we lose into things. A ring. A photograph. A stone. So that we never have to finish losing them.”
He was quiet for a moment.
“That is not love. That is keeping. Love lets go. Keeping polishes.”
“The second thing is about your daughter.”
I felt it then. Something cold that started at the back of my neck and went down.

“She wrote to me,” he said. “The week you came. She found my letter on your computer, on the kitchen table, where you had left it open. Come. Bring nothing. She found my address. She wrote me a letter by hand and sent it by post, and it came here eleven days after you did.” He laid one finger on the old envelope. “She asked me to let her mother go.”
I could not speak.

“But it was not mine to let go,” he said. “A man can only give away what is his. Your wife was yours to give back to the sea. And you never would have done it with your eyes open. I knew that the first morning, when you stood in my door with your wet shoes and your broken wrist. I knew it from the letter. Every sentence the same length.”
He looked at me then.
“So I let you do it with your eyes closed.”

I did not understand. I want to tell you that honestly. For a moment I did not understand at all. I sat on the stool and looked at him and the words went past me like a car on the road below the house.
Then I understood.
“The lesson,” I said. “The fire.”
“Yes.”
“The stone you gave me. In the tongs. The cheap lab stone. Worth nothing.”
“Yes.”
“That was—“

“That was your wife,” said Elias. “The laboratory sent her here, as you asked. I signed for her. I sent you across the river for oil. When you came back, I put a different stone on the felt and told you it was her. I kept her in my shirt pocket for three weeks, in a white paper, until you were ready. Then I put her in your hands, and you held her in the flame, and you watched her turn to light.”
He did not look away.
“You said it was beautiful. You were right. It was the only goodbye you were able to make. So I made it possible.”

I do not remember standing up. I remember that I was standing, and the stool was on its side on the floor behind me, and my hands were on the edge of the long table, gripping it, and the table was shaking because I was shaking.
“You burned her.”
“No,” he said. “You did. I held the torch.”
“She was in your pocket. For three weeks. You walked around with her in your shirt—“
“Yes.”
“I breathed her.” I heard myself say it. “You said, you are breathing some of it now. I breathed her in. In this room.”

“Yes,” said Elias. “You did. She is in this room still. In your lungs, and mine, and the walls, and the rain. A little. That is where carbon goes. That is where all of us go, in the end.” He folded his hands. “It was the kindest place I could think of. Kinder than a box. Kinder than a ring.”
“Sit down,” he said. “There is a third thing.”
I did not sit down. He waited. He waited the way he had waited for my hands to learn to hold a stone, the way he waited for the light. In the end, I picked up the stool, and sat.
“The third thing,” he said, “is about the Kono stone.”

He looked at the stone on the felt between us. The yellow one. The honey-coloured one. The one I had worked on for two years. The one with my fingertip in it. The one with thirty-one memories in it, and one I could not see.
“For twenty-eight years I looked for clean hands to cut it,” he said. “There are no clean hands, Kian. Not mine. Not yours. Not anyone’s. So I chose hands that did not know.”
I looked at the stone.
“A man who does not know what he is holding,” said Elias, “cuts with love. That is all I needed from you. Your love. For two years. Pointed at the wrong stone.”
I looked at it for a long time.
Fifty-seven faces. Every angle where Tolkowsky said it should be. The fire moving inside it from room to room, turning on lights.
Whose house is this, she had said, in the window, in the soft yellow light. This isn’t my house.
The grey cloth on the top shelf of the safe, a finger’s width to the left.
Clean hands are only hands that do not know what they are holding.
Short sleeves, or long sleeves?

I had read the story the night before, in my room above the wine shop. Elias had left it for me on the long table when I went home at eleven, in an envelope with my name on it, typed, six pages. I had read it at midnight. I had thought it was about someone else.
“The man in the white car,” I said.
“Yes,” said Elias.

He did not say anything else for a while. Neither did I. The north window was going grey now, the first light coming up over the roofs of the diamond quarter, the first tram bell ringing far away round the station square.
“Why,” I said at last. “Why not you. Why not cut it yourself, if you wanted it cut.”

“Because I could not have cut it with love,” he said. “I could only have cut it with what I felt on that road. And a stone cut that way would have been dark. You have seen a dark stone. The light leaks out of the bottom.” He touched the felt beside it. “This one is not dark. You made it beautiful. You made it the most beautiful stone I have seen come out of this street in fifty years. That is what it was owed.”
“Owed.”
“Yes. Owed.” He looked at me steadily. “A thing that cost what it cost should not also be ugly. That would be two crimes.”
“I did not do this to hurt you,” he said.
He said it plainly, the way he said everything.

“I did it because it was true. Your wife wanted the sea. Your daughter wanted her mother back. The stone wanted a cutter. You wanted something to cut. I had all four in this room. I gave each of them what they asked for.” He spread his thin hands on the table. “Two people asked me for something. I gave you both what you asked. That is not the same as hurting you. Most people go to their graves without learning the difference.”
“And what did you want?”
He was silent for a long time.
“To stop,” he said.
“Every stone carries one tension,” he said. “I told you that on the first day. I said you would understand it on the last day and not before. This is the last day.”
He looked at me with his very dark, very still eyes.
“Find it before you cut,” he said, “or it finds you.”
He pushed the old envelope across the table toward me, very slowly, with one finger.
“Yours,” he said, “was never in the diamond.”
The Letter

The envelope was addressed in blue ink, in a girl’s careful capitals, to MR ELIAS KARAM, at the address in the diamond quarter. The stamps were American. The postmark was from the town at the bottom of the canyon, two years before. It had been opened once, neatly, along the top, with a knife, and then closed again, and sealed with a strip of clear tape.
On the back, in the same blue ink, she had written: Please give this to my father when he finishes. Not before.
Inside were four pages torn from a school exercise book. The same kind I had kept under my pillow in a basement in Tehran.

And a second sheet, folded separately, newer, whiter, in a different pen. Elias pushed the thin envelope across to me too. “That one came last week,” he said. “She sent it to be put in with the first. I did not read it.”
I unfolded the four old pages. Somewhere in the last hour I had picked the stone up again. It was in my other hand. I did not know I was holding it until I read the first line.
Baba,
If the man in Belgium does what I ask, you’ll read this when your stone is finished. You’ll probably be holding it.
Put it down. I mean it. Put it down first.
I put it down. On the felt. My hand did it without me.

I’m writing this on Mom’s side of the bed, because it’s the last place in the house that still smells like her. It’s going. Every night there’s a little less. Kaveh comes in around three and gets under the covers, and we lie there and breathe in turns, like we’re stealing it from each other.
You took her on a Tuesday. I came home and went into the living room to say goodnight to her like I always did, and I picked up the box, and I knew right away, because it was lighter.

Do you know how I knew what it weighed? Because I’d been sleeping with it. Every night since they gave her back. I took it off the shelf after you went to bed and I slept with it under my arm, like I was five, and I put it back before you got up. Every night. You never noticed. You notice everything, Baba. You notice if a violin is a hair flat. You didn’t notice that.
You opened her with Grandma’s gold spoon. It was on the counter with grey on it. You didn’t even wash it.
So I did something, and I’m telling you because you should know what you turned us into.
I put my finger in what was left of her, and I put it in my mouth.

It tasted like chalk and pennies and nothing. I did it again the next night. And the next. And the next. Until Grandma caught me, in the kitchen, at two in the morning, with my finger in my mouth and the box open on the counter, and she didn’t shout. She sat down on the floor. She sat down right on the kitchen floor and cried so hard she couldn’t get up, and I had to sit down with her, and we sat there on the tiles until it was light.
I wanted some of her somewhere you couldn’t get a spoon into.
Some of her is in me now, Baba. You can’t cut me.

Mom wanted the ocean. She said it on the beach at Zuma, that last summer, when I was teaching Kaveh to swim. I saw her from the water. I couldn’t hear the words but I saw her look out at us and say something, and later in the car she told me. “Past the kelp,” she said. “Where you learned to swim. That’s where I want to go.” She said she’d told you. You were right there. You were on your phone.
You never heard anything that wasn’t a season.

Kaveh made a calendar on the fridge like Mom’s. Just squares. He crosses one off every night before bed. He doesn’t put a number at the bottom because he doesn’t know how many there will be. He asked me how many there would be and I told him I didn’t know, and he said, “Then I’ll just keep drawing them.”

He’s stopped talking much. He’s started sorting things. Everything. His Lego, his pencils, the spoons in the drawer. If something is in the wrong place he gets so upset he shakes. You know what that is. Mom knew what it was. Grandma knows. There’s nobody left in this house who knows what to do about it.
He’s yours, Baba. That’s what Mom said at Nowruz. “He’s yours.” She said it like a weather report. She was right. He’s yours, and you left him.
Now the car.
Nobody has ever said this to you. Grandma said don’t. The lawyer said don’t. The police said you were in shock. The therapist they sent me to said you’d get there when you were ready.
You never got there. You went to Belgium instead.

Mom texted me at 2:41 that night. I was awake, because you two were laughing so loud in the garage I could hear it through the floor. I still have it. I read it every day. I’m going to copy it exactly, so you can’t say you don’t remember.
“Dad’s driving her first. He promised slow. Go to sleep monkey. Love you.”
Mom never drove that car.
You never let anyone touch it.
You told me so yourself. In the garage. “Nobody drives it but me. Not even your mother.”

You’d been awake for two days. She knew. That text is the last thing she ever said to me, and it says she knew, and she went anyway. Because she loved your seasons more than she loved being careful. Because it was the end of one and she wanted to be there for the end, the way she always was, so she could write Welcome back.
I hate her for that a little. I’ve never said that to anyone. I’ve never even said it to myself out loud. Now I’ve said it to you, so now you have to carry it too.
I’m going to write to the man in Belgium. I found his letter on your laptop. “Come. Bring nothing.” You didn’t even close it.

I’m going to ask him to let her go. I’m going to ask him to do to you what you did to us. Take her while you’re not looking. I don’t know if he will. I don’t know what he can do. I don’t want to know.
If he does it, then I did it. Not him. Me.
So hate me, Baba. But hate me exactly the right amount.
Not more.
I love you.

That’s the worst part of this letter. I’ve been trying to stop since you left. Every day. I try to put it down like you put things down when a season ends. I can’t. It’s the one thing I can’t put down.
— S.
I sat at the long table with the four pages in my hands.
I could not see them any more. My eyes had stopped working. Elias had not moved. The north window had gone from grey to white. The tram bell rang again round the station square.
And the curve came back.

Not the curve the way I had remembered it for two years. Not her in the driver’s seat, pulling it forward because she was shorter, laughing at how low it was, her bare feet on the pedals. That had never happened. I knew it, suddenly, the way you know the grain of a stone, all at once, without searching. It had never happened. I had built it. Facet by facet, in a hospital bed in Pasadena, because a man can build anything when he has to, and I had polished it until there was no scar on it at all.
What came back was this.

My hands on the wheel. The thin wooden wheel of a 1967 car, smooth under my palms. The keys in the ignition, where I had put them. Roxana beside me, in the passenger seat, in my old university sweatshirt, with her arm out of the window and the cold air pushing against her hand. Singing something under her breath. The orange field of the city falling away below us. The stars coming out.
The forty hours.

How heavy my eyes were. How I was so happy, so warm, so finished, that I let them close. For one second. Only one. On a straight piece of road, before the curve, because the summit was behind me, because the season was done, because for the first time in three years I could rest.
The headlights sweeping across a wall of rock.
My hands gripping the wheel. Hard. Bracing. You usually see it when someone’s holding on to something hard.
The bruise across my chest, from my left shoulder down to my right hip. The driver’s belt.
The officer in the hospital, writing in his notebook, not looking at me.
My mother at the window, who did not turn around.
I folded the four pages, very slowly, along their old creases. My hands knew the way.
Then I opened the second sheet. The new one. The different pen.
P.S. — Different pen. I’m seventeen now. Elias says you’re nearly done.

He had forty-one jars by the end, Baba. Kaveh. Forty-one jars of Lego by colour along his wall, and if one piece was wrong he screamed until he threw up on the carpet. Every night. For a year. Grandma and I took turns sitting with him.
In October we scattered what you left of her. Past the kelp, at Zuma, where I learned to swim and where I taught him. We didn’t wait for you. Grandma said we’d waited long enough.

Kaveh held her. The bag, in both hands. He wouldn’t let anyone else. He held it so tight and so long his hands went white, and then he opened it and let go, all at once, and she went into the water, and he watched her go.
He doesn’t sort the Lego anymore. He gave the jars to the library in the canyon, the one where Mom used to teach, so other kids could build things.
Now he counts waves.
He counted four hundred and twelve that day, and he wouldn’t get back in the car until he’d finished. He goes every Saturday. Grandma drives him. He sits on the sand and counts until it gets dark.
He’s eleven, Baba.
Come home before he learns how to leave.
Arithmetic
I do not know how long I sat there.
Long enough for the light to change twice. Long enough for the tram bell to ring many times. Long enough for my hands to stop shaking, and then start again, and then stop.

Elias did not move. He sat across the long table from me with his thin hands folded, and waited, the way he waited for everything. Once, he got up, slowly, and made tea in the two glasses after all, and put one in front of me, and sat back down. I did not drink it. It went cold.
“I want to hit you,” I said at last.
“Then hit me,” said Elias. “If it would help.”
“Would it?”
“No.” He looked at me. “It would only give you something to do. You have always needed something to do. That is how we came here.”
I did not hit him.
“What happens to it,” I said. “The stone.”
He looked at it, on the felt between us, still burning in the white light from the window.
“It will be sold,” he said. “This week. A man is coming on Thursday. It will fetch a great deal of money. More than anything else that has ever left this room.”
“And you’ll keep it.”
“No.” He shook his head very slightly. “I have found him.”
“Found who?”

“The boy,” said Elias. “From the road. He is a man now. Thirty-eight years old. He lives in Freetown. He has a wife, and two daughters, and a small shop where he repairs mobile telephones, with one hand. It took me nine years and a great deal of money to find him, and I found him six years ago, and I have known his name every day since.” He was quiet for a moment. “Every cent the stone fetches will go to him. Through a lawyer, so he never has to see my face. He will not know where it came from. He will only know that one day his life changed.”
“Is that justice?” I said.
Elias thought about it. He thought about it honestly, the way he thought about a stone, with all of his attention, for a long time.
“No,” he said. “It is arithmetic.”
He unfolded his hands and laid them flat on the table.

“There is no justice for what happened on that road,” he said. “Nothing I do now can make it not have happened. Money does not grow a hand back. But a stone that cost a hand should not make a buyer rich. So the hand gets the stone. That is all. It is not forgiveness. It is not justice. It is only the numbers on both sides of the page coming out even.” He looked at me. “I have been a buyer all my life, Kian. Arithmetic is the only honest thing I know how to do.”
“You could have stopped it,” I said. “On the road. You could have said something.”
“Yes.”
“Why didn’t you?”
He was silent for a long time. Longer than for any other question I had asked him in two years. When he answered, it was in the same voice, flat and even. But it was quieter.
“Because I was looking at the stone,” he said.
He looked down at his hands.

“I had my loupe to my eye, and the light was going into it, and the world went quiet. The way it goes quiet for you. The way it went quiet for you in the basement in Tehran with your exercise book, while your mother asked you to hold her hand. I heard the question. Short or long. I heard it. And I was looking at the stone, and the quiet was so beautiful, and I did not want to come out of it. That is the whole truth. There is no other part.”
He raised his eyes to mine.

“There is a sentence every buyer on that road told himself,” he said. “If I do not buy it, someone else will. It was true. It is still true. It is the sentence I have said to myself every night for twenty-eight years. And it is the sentence I will die with, because it is true, and it does not help at all.”
I picked up the stone.
I held it up, one last time, to the north window. The fire moved inside it from room to room, turning on lights. Red. Orange. A blue so pure it hurt. Violet. Gold.
Fifty-seven faces. Thirty-one of them named for a woman who was not inside it. One named for a sentence I had never heard. And all of them cut, with love, into the price of a child’s hand.
It was the most beautiful thing I had ever made.
I put it down on the felt. I pushed it, very gently, with one finger, across the table toward him.
“It’s not mine,” I said.
“No,” said Elias. “It never was.”

He stood up then. Slowly. It took him a long time. He was so thin now that his white shirt seemed to stand on its own around him. He went to the north window and stood there looking down into the street, the way he had stood every day at noon with his apple.
“I will not see the spring,” he said.

I did not ask him how he knew. I did not ask him if he was ill. I knew he was not ill. I knew exactly what he was. He was a man whose engine had found the one thing it wanted at five years old, and had held it for seventy-six years, and had at last, this morning, set it down.
A man who finishes everything has nowhere to stand.
I will cut it when I am ready to stop.
“You’ll be alone,” I said.

“I have always been alone,” he said. “That is not the same as lonely. Men like us confuse the two all our lives.” He turned his head and looked at me over his shoulder. “You are not alone. That is the difference between us. That is the only difference that matters. Go home.”

“What if I can’t?” I said. “What if I go home and it starts again. The engine. What if I stand in the door and I’m already looking for the next thing. I was looking for it yesterday. You saw me. Within the hour. I was looking at your safe.”
“Yes,” said Elias. “I saw.”
“So what do I do?”
He turned back to the window.

“You choose,” he said. “We never stop wanting. We only learn to choose what we want. I told you that. It took me seventy years and a child’s hand to learn it. You have learned it in two years, and it cost you a fingertip and your wife and very nearly your children.” He was quiet for a moment. “You got it cheaper than I did. Do not waste it.”
I put on my coat.

I stood in the open steel doorway of the empty workshop for a moment, with my one bag over my shoulder, the way I had stood there on the first morning with my wet shoes. He was at the north window with his back to me. The stone was on the felt on the long table, burning quietly in the morning light. The green safe stood open and empty in the wall.
“Elias,” I said.
He did not turn round.
“Bring nothing,” he said.

I went down the four flights of stairs, and out of the steel door, and past the cameras, and past the young officer in the booth, who lifted two fingers to me from behind the glass for the last time, and out between the steel posts into the street.
It was raining.
The Door
The flight was eleven hours. I did not sleep. I did not read. I did not count anything.
I sat by the window with my hands in my lap, the left one with its short flat fingertip on top, and looked out at the white floor of cloud. And for the first time in my life, I let the dead air come.

I did not fight it. I did not look for something to put in front of it. I let it come in and fill me, the empty loud quiet, the engine running with nothing to hold, and I sat inside it, and I felt it, all of it, the whole terrible weight of a mind with nothing to do. For eleven hours.
It did not kill me. That surprised me. All my life I had believed it would.

I want to tell you that it was peaceful. It was not. Somewhere over Greenland the engine began, very quietly, to look for something. It went to the safe in Antwerp, and I brought it back. It went to the mathematics of light, and I brought it back. It went to the car, and how I could have taken the curve, and the exact angle of the steering wheel, and I brought it back. Again and again. Like a dog that keeps going to the door.
Every time, I brought it back to the same place. To a small sheet of exercise paper, taped to a fridge with too much tape, with squares drawn on it in pencil all the way down to the bottom edge.
I did not know if that was choosing. I thought it might be. I thought it might be the beginning of it.

My mother met me at the airport. She was smaller than I remembered. Older. She had driven herself, in her old car, the one she had refused to let me replace for fifteen years, and she was standing at the barrier in arrivals in her good coat, holding her handbag in front of her with both hands.
She saw me. She saw my face, and my hand, and the one bag over my shoulder, and nothing else in my arms.
She did not ask about the stone.
She put her arms around me, at the barrier, in front of everybody, and held on. She was shaking. She was saying something into my coat, very quietly, in Persian, the same thing over and over.
It was the sentence. The one from the kitchen two years ago, when she had found the spoon. The one that went past me like a car on the road below the house.
I heard it this time.
Your father left the hole open, she was saying. Your father left the hole open. Your father left the hole open, Kian.
We drove up the canyon in the late afternoon. Neither of us spoke. The oaks. The dirt road. The long low house at the end of it, with the view down toward the sea.
She did not park in front of the garage. She parked by the kitchen door.

In the hallway, on the floor, just inside the front door, there was a small carpet. A prayer rug. Old, faded, a hundred years old at least, with a garden pattern in red and walnut brown and the blue that is almost black. My father’s rug from Tehran. My mother had brought it up from Encino and laid it there, in my house, sometime in the two years I had been gone.
In its corner, the hole.
I stood on it. I knelt down. I put my finger in the hole, the short flat one, and felt the edges of it, the old knots frayed and soft where they stopped.
I understood it then. Thirty years late.

A man who could mend a hundred-year-old carpet so that nobody could ever find the scar, and he left one hole open in his own rug. Not because he did not have the time. Because some holes are not damage. Some holes are the shape of what was there. Mend them perfectly, and the people who walk on it forget. A carpet, my father said, forgets nothing. It was the people he worried about.

He kept the hole so that he could put his finger in it, in America, and remember. Tehran. The shop. The bazaar. The basement. The war. Everything he could not bring. He did not make it into something else. He did not polish it. He let it be a hole, and he let it hurt, and he kept it near the door, where he would step on it every day.
I had spent two years trying to make my wife into a stone with no scar on it.

I stood up. My knees ached. My mother was standing behind me in the hall, with her handbag in front of her in both hands, watching me with her basement face. But it was a different basement face. I could not have said how. I think, now, it was the face of a woman in a basement who has just heard the radio say the other words. The white situation. The face of a woman who does not yet believe them.
“They’re inside,” she said.
I did not go in through the kitchen. I do not know why. I went back out, and round the side of the house, and up the three stone steps to the front door. And I stood there.

I did not knock. I stood on the step in the late light, with the canyon going gold behind me and the sea below, the grey-blue that goes almost black, and I could hear, through the door, very faintly, my son’s voice. Counting.

He was counting something. I could not hear what. The numbers came through the wood, steady, flat, in order, one after another, the way I had counted tiles in a basement forty years ago and seconds between a siren and a sound.
Four hundred and nine. Four hundred and ten. Four hundred and eleven.
And I felt it.

I want to be honest, here, at the end, as I have tried to be everywhere. I felt the engine catch. I felt the old warm water. Standing on that step, with my son’s voice coming through the door, I felt my mind begin to narrow, the world begin to go quiet around one thing, the lights going down in the cinema. I felt it reach for him. The way it had reached for the cube, and the board, and the firm, and the car, and the stone. The hook. Already.
My son.

I stood very still. I let it come. I did not know, standing there, whether this was the beginning of the most important season of my life or the beginning of the worst thing I would ever do to him. I did not know whether a person can be a season. Whether a man like me can point the engine at a child, and hold it there, and never let it narrow so far that the child becomes an interruption. Whether I could look at my son for the rest of my life and never once try to find the crack in him. Never once try to polish it out.
I did not know. I want to be honest. I did not know at all.
We never stop wanting. We only learn to choose what we want.
The counting stopped.
There were footsteps in the hall. Not Kaveh’s. Lighter. Faster. Older.
The door opened.

Sahar was standing in it. She was taller than me now, or nearly. She was seventeen. Her hair was tied up with a pencil stuck through it. She was wearing my old university sweatshirt, the one that had been her mother’s, the one the hospital had given back to my mother in a plastic bag, washed now, soft, the sleeves pushed up to the elbows.
She did not say anything. She looked at me. At my face. At my empty hands. At the short flat end of my finger.

Behind her, at the end of the hall, by the window that looks down the canyon toward the sea, a boy was standing with his back to the glass. He was eleven. He had his mother’s eyes and his hair stuck up at the back where he had slept on it, and he was holding a thick stack of exercise paper, taped together end to end, so long it trailed down onto the floor and across the carpet. Seven hundred and thirty squares. Every one with a neat cross in it. No number at the bottom.
He was looking at me. His lips had stopped moving.
I stood on the step.
I had brought nothing.
I had room.
My daughter stood in the door and looked at me, and waited, the way her mother had waited, the way Elias had waited, for weather, for light, for a stone to show where it wanted to open.
I did not know if she would let me in.
I did not know if I would stay.
I looked at her. Only at her. I did not look past her. I did not look for the crack.
And I lifted my foot from the step.

GLOSSARY
Baba [baa-BAA] — Persian, dad. What Kian’s children call him.
Boart [BORT] — The trade word for industrial diamonds of poor colour and shape, crushed into powder for saws, drills and the paste on a polishing wheel.
Brilliance — The white light a well-cut diamond sends back out of its top.
Bruting [BROO-ting] — Grinding one diamond against another to round its outline. The oldest part of the cutter’s craft.
Carat [KA-rat] — The unit of a diamond’s weight. One carat is a fifth of a gram, named after the carob seeds once used as weights in Middle Eastern and Mediterranean markets.
Chehelom [che-he-LOM] — Persian, the fortieth. The gathering held forty days after a death, which closes the first and hardest part of mourning.
Cleaving [KLEE-ving] — Splitting a diamond along its natural grain with one blow. The English word also means to hold on to someone tightly, as in the old marriage vows.
Cloud — A haze of tiny dots trapped inside a diamond, too small to see one by one.
Crown — The upper part of a cut diamond, above its widest edge.
Culet [KYOO-let] — The point at the very bottom of a cut diamond.
Dead air — Kian’s name for the empty stretch after an obsession ends. A radio term for the silence when a station has nothing to broadcast.
Dey [DAY] — The tenth month of the Persian calendar, falling in the deep of winter, from late December to late January.
Facet [FA-set] — One flat, polished face of a cut stone. A round brilliant diamond has fifty-seven, or fifty-eight with a culet.
Feather — A small, flat crack inside a diamond, white and frayed at the edges like a feather frozen in ice.
Fire — The flashes of colour a cut diamond throws by splitting white light, the way a glass prism does.
Frances Gerety [GERR-uh-tee] — The American copywriter who wrote the slogan “A Diamond Is Forever” in 1947.
Freetown — The capital of Sierra Leone, on the Atlantic coast, founded as a home for freed slaves.
Ganzfeld effect [GANTS-felt] — German, whole field. The brain’s habit of inventing shapes, faces and places when the eyes see nothing but an even, unchanging field of light for a long time.
Girdle — The thin outer edge of a cut diamond, where the crown meets the pavilion.
Gujarati [goo-ja-RAA-tee] — The language of Gujarat, on the western coast of India, spoken by many families in the diamond trade.
Haft-sin [haft-SEEN] — Persian, seven S’s. The table laid for the
Persian New Year with seven things whose names begin with the letter S.
HPHT — High pressure, high temperature. A machine that grows diamonds from carbon by squeezing and heating it as the deep earth does.
Kimberley Process [KIM-ber-lee] — The international scheme, begun in 2003, meant to keep diamonds that pay for rebel wars out of the trade. Named after the South African town where it was agreed.
Kimberlite [KIM-ber-lite] — The volcanic rock that carries diamonds up from about a hundred and fifty kilometres underground, named after Kimberley in South Africa.
Koh-i-Noor [KOH-ee-NOOR] — Persian, mountain of light. A great diamond fought over by kings for centuries, now in the British crown jewels.
Kono [KOH-noh] — A diamond-mining district in the east of Sierra
Leone, and the place Elias was born.
Lavoisier [la-VWAH-zee-ay] — Antoine Lavoisier, the French chemist who burned a diamond in the 1770s and proved it was made of carbon.
Loupe [LOOP] — A small magnifying glass, usually ten times, held right up to the eye.
Memorial diamond — A diamond grown in a laboratory using carbon taken from a person’s remains or hair.
Motor-e kuchik [mo-TOR-e koo-CHEEK] — Persian, little engine.
Kian’s mother’s name for his mind.
Needle — A long, thin crystal of another mineral lying inside a diamond like a pin.
Nader Shah [naa-DER SHAAH] — The Persian king who took Delhi in 1739 and, by legend, named the Koh-i-Noor.
Nowruz [now-ROOZ] — Persian, new day. The Persian New Year, on the first day of spring.
Octahedron [ok-ta-HEE-dron] — Greek, eight faces. The shape a diamond most likes to grow in: two four-sided pyramids joined at their bases.
Ordibehesht [or-dee-be-HESHT] — The second month of the
Persian calendar, from late April to late May.
Pavilion — The lower, cone-shaped part of a cut diamond, below its widest edge.
Pinpoint — A single tiny speck of light or dark inside a diamond.
Retort — The furnace chamber in which a body is cremated. The name comes from the glass vessel an alchemist heated over a flame.
RUF — The Revolutionary United Front, the rebel army in Sierra
Leone’s civil war from 1991 to 2002, known for cutting off civilians’ hands.
Scaife [SKAYF] — The cutter’s polishing wheel: a flat iron disc spinning about three thousand times a minute, coated with diamond dust and olive oil.
Scintillation [sin-ti-LAY-shun] — The sparkle of light and dark across a cut diamond as it, or the person looking at it, moves.
Seasons — Roxana’s name for Kian’s obsessions.
Sierra Leone [see-AIR-ah lee-OHN] — A small country on the
Atlantic coast of West Africa.
Star facets — The eight small triangular faces around the table of a cut diamond.
Table — The large flat face on the top of a cut diamond, where the light comes in.
Tolkowsky [tol-KOV-skee] — Marcel Tolkowsky, the Antwerp-born engineer who worked out the ideal angles for a round diamond in 1919.
Vaz’iyat-e ghermez [vaz-ee-YAT-e gher-MEZ] — Persian, the red situation. The radio’s name for an air-raid alert in wartime
Tehran.
Vaz’iyat-e sefid [vaz-ee-YAT-e se-FEED] — Persian, the white situation. The radio’s all-clear.
